speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY
speechtext: It is the practice for the Speaker to inform the house about messages that he receives. Needless to say, I am pleased to inform the house that today is the birthday of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister. I am sure I express the views of everyone when I wish him a very happy birthday and many happy returns of the day.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY
speechtext:
May I avail myself of the privilege, with the consent of the house, of extending to the Prime Minister the warmest good wishes for many happy returns of his birthday. One of the happy incidents of service in the House of Commons is that the contacts we make with each other leave no doubt in our minds about the sincerity with which those of different political views seek to serve the common cause. With that in mind we extend our friendship and our personal contacts, but always reserving, as we always shall, the right to disagree. That is a healthy state of affairs.
I extend good wishes to the Prime Minister not only for his health and happiness on the occasion of his birthday but also for the trip ahead of him. May I remind hon. members that the Prime Minister, looking extremely well, is, after all, still a comparative youngster when one compares his age with that of the very youthful head of another government of the commonwealth with whom he will be lunching in just a few days. In extending our good wishes to him today, may I express the hope that for long years ahead his health, vigour and happiness may continue.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY
speechtext:
I wish to thank you, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition and all my colleagues for these expressions of good wishes, the sincerity of which I find very touching. It is one of the perhaps not too many satisfactions of public life to be able to vigorously prosecute one's own opinions and ideas and still feel that one retains the esteem of those with whom one is trying
to serve the state. We all welcome every opportunity to exchange warm good wishes with each other on proper occasions, and thereby to show each other that we do appreciate the sincerity of each of us in endeavouring to serve our great country to the best of our individual ability.

subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do want to say that I am sure all of us, irrespective of our political views, join with the Leader of the Opposition, the Speaker and everyone else in extending our good wishes to the Prime Minister. When we say this sort of thing sometimes some people, because of our political differences, think that there is some insincerity about it, but I want to say that I am confident that there is no insincerity anywhere in the house in wishing the Prime Minister health, happiness and many happy returns of the day.

subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON BIRTHDAY
speechtext: I am very glad, Mr. Speaker, that there are occasions when it is possible for us to forget our differences and emphasize the common ground on which we stand. Birthdays seem to be one of those occasions, and I am very happy to be able at this time to join the other hon. gentlemen who have spoken in extending to the Prime Minister our very warmest wishes for many happy returns of the day and to assure him that there must be many hon. members who hope that at 72 they will be as spry as the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, since the full text may not have been available to all hon. members, I thought I might table the official text of the communique issued at the conclusion of the meeting of commonwealth finance ministers in Australia which ended on the 15th of January. There is little I can add, or perhaps should add, to what is in the communique. As the house knows, this was the most recent of a series of meetings that have been held at fairly regular intervals since the end of the war. At these meetings the questions which have been discussed have related primarily
1S24	HOUSE OF
Commonwealth Finance Conference to the commonwealth countries in the sterling area. As the house is aware, the United Kingdom acts as banker for and holds the reserves of the sterling area countries. As a result of conditions arising out of the war, sterling has been inconvertible up to the present time, and it has been necessary to impose a variety of restrictions upon trade.
I have had the privilege of attending all these meetings since the end of the war. In my opinion this last meeting was, in many ways, one of the most satisfactory of any of them.
The questions reviewed were the progress made in liberalizing trade and in moving towards the goal of convertibility. The targets were set two years ago, at a time of real crisis, and they were reaffirmed at the meeting a year ago. Anyone who has watched the march of events will realize there has been a moderate but steady improvement during all that period. Today sterling is stronger than it has been at any time since the end of the war, and there has been a progressive liberalization of all these trade restrictions.
I am happy to say that at the meeting in Sydney the goals of freer trade and convertibility were reaffirmed.
I have always hesitated to assume the role of prophet, and I do not presume to do so now. The time when sterling, one of the world's great trading currencies, is made convertible must of course be determined by those who are primarily responsible for that currency. But in my opinion, that goal is very much nearer than any one of us would have dared to hope even as short a time since as a year ago.
I should like to add one word, and that is to say that the arrangements made by our host, the Australian government, were admirable in every respect. The Australian Prime Minister, Mr. Menzies, who presided, did so with his usual ability and tact. The hospitality which was extended to us by our Australian friends was beyond praise. I regret that because of a minor throat affliction I was not able to participate to the extent to which I would have liked. Nevertheless, I can assure you that the hospitality was fully up to what I had always heard were Australian standards, so that all in all I found it was a most satisfactory conference.
Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe
Opposition): In view of the insistence with which we have presented requests in this house at different times, Mr. Speaker, in the form of resolutions seeking the initiative in reaching the goal of convertibility, we will naturally welcome with great enthusiasm the statement that the goal of convertibility is so


much nearer. I must say that we welcome also the fact that convertibility has now become a respectable word. There was a time when ridicule was poured on the suggestion that our government might take the initiative in seeking ways to further the cause of convertibility. The Australian government, having taken the initiative, obviously has attained results which are satisfactory to the government. While we would regret that the initiative had not been taken in accordance with our resolution, we welcome this statement that the goal of convertibility is closer today than it was before.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT ON AWARDING OF CONTRACTS FOR BUILDING
speechtext:
On several occasions
recently, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has addressed questions to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) concerning the national film board, and the Prime Minister had answered, I think, on each occasion that the government was considering the awarding of a contract for the building of the headquarters and operational units. The house will recall that the Massey commission and the J. D. Woods and Gordon company, when they investigated the work of the board some years ago, both recommended that the board should be housed in one building rather than in the eight or nine places they now occupy, and in which they work under quite unsatisfactory conditions. These recommendations were passed upon by a committee of this house something less than two years ago.
In the meantime the government took steps to investigate the sites available, and a property was located in Ville St. Laurent and acquired at a price which, at the moment, has totalled about $256,000. It may cost up to $25,000 or perhaps $30,000 more to negotiate for the remaining pieces of property. At

this point invitations were extended by the Department of Public Works for tenders for the buildings, and several tenders were received, the lowest being $5,230,760. With the expenditure of that amount before it, the government has been considering this question to see if that expenditure is justified, having in mind the operations of the film board and as well the acknowledged fact that private industry in the film trade in Canada has been improving in the quality and quantity of its output. We did give serious consideration to this question, and came to the conclusion that the national film board was producing films of an educational and cultural nature which were providing real advantages to the Canadian people, and that if the film board did not produce these they could not be otherwise produced in Canada.
For that reason, we have decided that this advantage should be continued, and for the benefit of the Canadian people we have authorized the awarding of a contract to the lowest tender in the amount I have mentioned. May I say, sir, that I have only been responsible for the work of the film board in parliament for the past few months. In the study we have made during that time, we have been struck by the remarkably improved efficiency of the film board in the past few years and the much improved public relations which it seems to enjoy with the Canadian taxpayer. I cannot help but take this opportunity, sir, to say that in my opinion this is due not only to the good work of the employees and the present and former commissioners, but in particular to the supervisory and administrative skill of my predecessor, the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters).

Now, so far as the recommendations are concerned, they did not place before the house any comparative advantages as between Ottawa and any other city. And I wish to make it abundantly clear that I am not presuming to express an opinion as to where the less desirable site would be. We simply have no information before us.
Attempts that were made by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) to get information when this item came before the house last year, on April 9, 1953, indicate just how little was available. On that occasion the hon. member for Peterborough pressed the minister responsible for information as to what was contemplated. Let us take a couple of examples just to see how little this house knew about what was then taking place. In response to a question put at that time the minister said, as reported at page 3645 of Hansard:
I am not too sure we have completed purchase of the site.
If he was not, who would be? Then he went on to say:
I think somebody raised that question earlier in the session and I answered that we were negotiating with two or three parties who are the owners of the site.
This, mark you, was on the occasion when these main estimates were before the house for consideration, a time when, we have been told, the house made a decision in this matter.
Then, on another occasion, when the minister was asked what he thought it would cost, he said:
I am told that the whole project will cost approximately $5 million . . . We have not completed the purchase of the land and I would not like to give the figures I have here at this time.

That is the last time there was any opportunity for members of this house to obtain positive information. The item passed in the absence of that information.
Then an announcement was subsequently made that a decision had been taken to move this to Ville St. Laurent. That may be an excellent decision or it may not, depending upon what the reasons are; and this house surely has a right to know what reasons motivated the government in coming to that decision.
We have tried on a number of occasions, as hon. members will recall, to obtain information. Hon. members will recall that in the debate on the speech from the throne, when I spoke in opening the debate, I pointed out the absence of information on something which not only involved an expenditure of money but had very important cultural features in connection with it as embraced in the Massey commission's report, to which reference has already been made. My request at that time was denied. No steps were taken to carry out my suggestion.
Then, on January 19 of this year, I directed the attention of the Prime Minister to a press report which had just appeared respecting the national film board, which said that the government was reconsidering its decision. I asked the Prime Minister whether there would be an opportunity to discuss the matter further. His reply, as reported at page 1235 of Hansard, is as follows:
There has been no decision reached in that matter. What is under consideration at the present time is the tenders that were submitted for the construction of a building in Montreal. They are all of a very substantial amount, and the matter that is now under consideration is as to whether or not the government will recommend the appropriations required for that large expenditure at this time.
I then asked:
Do I understand from what the Prime Minister has said that, having regard to the amount involved, the government may actually be reconsidering whether it will or will not move the national film board from Ottawa?
To that the Prime Minister replied:
No decision has been reached in that regard, but until the government comes to parliament with a definite recommendation for a definite amount to be expended for a building at a definite place there is always a possibility that changes in the recommendation may be made.
Now, there is both a question of propriety of procedure, and a question of the rights of parliament involved. The Prime Minister said at that time:
. . . until the government comes to parliament with a definite recommendation for a definite amount to be expended for a building at a definite place there is always a possibility that changes in the recommendation may be made.


Let us assume he thought that changes were not going to be made. It was said that the matter would be laid before parliament before changes were made.
Then, within a few days, in fact the very next day, I read a statement in the press by Mr. Gardiner-this was not the Minister of Agriculture but, I believe, an architect in the Department of Public Works.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON AWARDING OF CONTRACTS FOR BUILDING
speechtext: The chief architect.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON AWARDING OF CONTRACTS FOR BUILDING
speechtext:
The chief architect. He said that this matter was going to come before treasury board for recommendation. On that occasion I said:
In the late afternoon edition of the Ottawa Journal I read that the definite recommendation in regard to the adoption of a tender for the construction of the national film board building was definitely going to the treasury board. It seems to me that these statements are inconsistent. Having regard to the general principle involved and the assurance by the Prime Minister that we would have something before us before this move was definite, it seems to me that we should know what the situation is.
To that the Prime Minister replied:
I would hope that the house would take the statements made by the government in the house in preference to speculative reports by newspapers.
And hon. members in the house on that occasion will I am sure recall the firmness with which the Prime Minister made that statement and the hilarious applause with which his supporters in parliament greeted what was intended to be a rebuke made concerning even the very suggestion that anything contrary to what had been said on January 19 was contemplated.
I feel sure that the Prime Minister did not have the information before him when he made that statement. Then, today, we have the statement of the minister responsible for this, who blandly comes to the house and tells us this, in spite of the assurance by the Prime Minister that, "until the government comes to parliament with a definite recommendation for a definite amount to be expended for a building at a definite place, there is always a possibility that changes in the recommendation may be made".
I think this is a challenge to the rights of parliament concerning information in regard to the business of the people of Canada, and I say that a very real question of privilege arises in that members were misled-I am sure it was unintentional, because I feel sure the Prime Minister was sure that nothing had taken place at that time. But the fact is that now a statement is made by the minister in charge which confirms the announcement to which I referred earlier,

made by the chief architect in the Department of Public Works, that this was going to treasury board in any event.
I recall again the words of the Prime Minister, when that was pointed out to him:
I would hope that the house would take the statements made by the government In the house in preference to speculative reports by newspapers.
Unfortunately, those speculative reports, as they were called, turned out to be right. On the basis of the Prime Minister's statement, I submit that this house has a right to ask that the government reconsider this decision today. We do not pretend to be in a position to say where this building should go. We have been denied any information. The last time it was up for discussion we were told that the government did not have any plans, although they insisted on the item going through. We have no reasons before us why this should be done and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that both for the purpose of establishing the authority of parliament and for the purpose of doing the business of the people of Canada in an orderly manner, this should be reconsidered. It should be placed before the House of Commons, as was clearly implied by the Prime Minister in the statement on January 19.

Following representations that were offered, Mr. Speaker Macdonald gave the ruling I referred to, namely that when a minister makes a statement the leaders of the various groups will be allowed to reply.
Perhaps that is not the type of ruling that gives satisfaction because hon. members can always stand up and say that they have equal rights in the house. While the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), ministers of the government and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) may be considered to be in a different position under our rules, nevertheless the principal rule is that all hon. members are equal and have equal rights. Therefore, if one hon. member is allowed to speak, why should not I allow others to speak? speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. 176, to amend the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PREVENT INCREASE IN MAXIMUM RETIRING ALLOWANCE
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PREVENT INCREASE IN MAXIMUM RETIRING ALLOWANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the banking and commerce committee in 1952 recommended the bill which became the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act it was drafted in such a way that if an adjustment upward or downward was made subsequently to members' indemnities their contributions to the retiring fund and the matching contributions of the government


would be increased or decreased in the same proportion and so eventually would be the retiring allowances for those who ultimately became entitled to receive them.
It was felt that such proportionate adjustment in the contributions without any shortening of the period during which they were made would bring about a situation where the fund would remain actuarially sound and self-supporting, because only a small number of the many contributors were expected to ever become entitled to retiring allowances.
We have now reason to believe that that was the best kind of forecast that could be made at that time, but after all it was only a forecast and we do not think that there should be any automatic change in the contributions or ultimate possible effects at this time.
The purpose of this bill is to recommend amendments to the act to prevent any change in its operation or any increase in the maximum allowance from taking place automatically as a result of changes in the sessional indemnity proposed by Bill No. 171 now before us.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

1.	Has the government received a request from the provincial government of British Columbia, asking for the extension of P.F.R.A. facilities to that province? If so, when?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: P.F.R.A.-EXTENSION TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
1.	The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was passed in 1935 to provide for the rehabilitation of the drought and soil drifting areas in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta only. It enabled the undertaking, over a five-year period, of methods of farm practice and water development to minimize the very serious problems of drought and soil drifting that existed there at the time, in the area commonly referred to as the Palliser triangle.
An amendment in 1937 extended the activities to the withdrawal of poor lands from cultivation, and to the resettlement elsewhere, of farmers from such lands in the drought area. Provision was also made to organize those vacated lands into community pastures, and the act was further amended in 1939 removing the five-year time limitation but the pastures were confined to the drought area as above.
Representations have been made on a number of occasions in past years for the extension of the P.F.R.A. area to all of the prairie provinces as well as to British Columbia. The last request received from British Columbia was in a letter dated February 2, 1953, from Hon. R. E. Sommers, minister of lands and forests. The Minister of Agriculture replied to this letter on February 6, 1953, stating that the government has had this matter under consideration for some time and that until a decision had been reached specific problems in that province would be dealt with by special parliamentary appropriations as in the past.
In British Columbia a serious flood problem developed some years ago in the Lil-looet-Pemberton district. In response to representations from the province and the district a special parliamentary appropriation was provided over a number of years for the construction of flood control works and to March 31, 1953, the total expenditure was $1,163,811. Another parliamentary appropriation for special projects in British Columbia, that has been provided for a number of years, is that for the development of irrigation projects for the rehabilitation of veterans. Expenditures to March 31, 1953, under this vote amounted to $1,574,715, and

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that on April 27, 1953, as found at page 4444 of Hansard, I placed on the record a letter which had been written to the premier of Saskatchewan setting forth the government's position at that time. I do not think it is necessary for me to read the first half of the letter as it does not bear upon this particular point, but the last half does and I think I should read it again. Dealing with the report of the royal commission, it says:
The report has been tabled in the House of Commons and has given rise to very diverging views about the soundness of the project. Your government has prepared a document which is quite critical of the report and you have written the Prime Minister that your government feels the project should be proceeded with notwithstanding the report of the royal commission.
Since this is your view, the federal government is prepared to consider a definite proposal from the provincial government for co-operation in the project and I am authorized by my colleagues to discuss such a proposal with you once the question of water rights has been settled among the three prairie provinces and agreement reached that the water would be available for the project.
I may say in passing that the terms of that particular paragraph have since been met.
Any proposal put forward by the province should make it clear what contribution to the cost of the dam itself the province is prepared to make to remove any element of federal subsidy for the production of power since power development could obviously not be subsidized in one province unless the federal authorities were prepared to provide similar subsidies in all provinces and federal subsidies for power development are contrary to present government policy.
That is one of the paragraphs still under consideration, and which I presume the hon. member for Prince Albert has in mind in asking the question. I continue:
You will appreciate that any federal contribution would also have to be limited, as in the St. Mary's

Inquiries of the Ministry and Bow River projects, to works for the conservation of the water and that we could not justify the expenditure of money raised from taxes all over Canada until the provincial authorities had prepared a practical scheme for the distribution system which gave reasonable evidence that the water would actually be used for irrigation on a scale which would justify the expenditure of national funds.
The fifth paragraph reads as follows:
Any proposal would, of course, have to include some satisfactory means of determining in advance what the total cost of the project would be, and what the federal share of the cost would be. This would be essential so that there was no open-ended commitment which might result in the final costs being far greater than anything either government would regard as reasonable.
On these conditions as prerequisites the federal government is prepared to discuss the project further with the government of Saskatchewan.

Senate and House of Commons same indemnity as the members of this house? Since confederation, that has always been the case. Perhaps that, in itself, is not a sufficient reason. But what does appear to me to be a sufficient reason is that the four provinces stated, as expressly set out in the British North America Act, that it was their desire to be federally united into one dominion under the crown of the United Kingdom, Great Britain and Ireland, with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom. The parliament of the United Kingdom has been a two-chamber parliament as long as it has been a parliament, I believe-and that is for many centuries. The act itself, carrying out that principle, and that construction of the principle, provided that there shall be one parliament for Canada consisting of the queen, an upper house styled the Senate, and the House of Commons.
Now, that was the constitution that the fathers of confederation represented as being the one desired by the Canadian public. That constitution has operated now in this country for 87 years; and I, for one, feel grateful that the fathers of confederation did recommend at that time that the constitution for the parliament of this new federal dominion under the crown should be similar in principle to that of the parliament at Westminster. I think the parliament at Westminster has been the model of all successful democratic parliaments that have been established in the world since that time.
I know that questions have arisen from time to time about the portion of the work of parliament that is effectively done by the members of the Senate. Well, it must be recognized that the situations in the two houses are somewhat different and in consequence, though they both have responsibilities to the Canadian people, they have responsibilities of a different aspect concerning each of them.
We in this house are elected in our constituencies; the members in the other house are appointed. They are appointed, under the constitution, to their seats in the other house for life tenure. But because we are an elected chamber, then this chamber has the privilege, the right, the obligation and the responsibility of initiating all fiscal policies. And because we are elected it is our responsibility in this house-a responsibility that has been recognized from the earliest days of Canadian parliaments-to use this house as a forum where what takes place will help to form the opinion of the electorate of the country as to whether or not they should retain their confidence in those who constitute the government, or whether they
TMr. St. Laurent.]
should come to the conclusion that that government is no longer worthy of their confidence.
I think all of us will admit that a great many of the speeches made here in the house are intended for the purpose of properly informing the public in that respect, rather than because of any feeling as to the effect they will have upon the decision to be made in the house.
I am not complaining about that; I think that that is the proper working of democratic institutions. Those who support the government do so because they believe, and want their electors to believe, that the government is worthy of the public confidence. And the opposition has it as its duty to scrutinize very carefully the conduct and recommendations of the government. And I am quite sure they hope they would be able to do a better job, if they were on the government side of the house, than those who happen to be there. And, that being their belief, they try to promote that belief in the opinion of the country at large. That is the normal way in which these democratic institutions are intended to work, and the way in which they do work.
When we talk about streamlining our rules we have to keep in mind that those rules are not designed merely to get speedy disposition of the matters that come before parliament, but that they must also be designed to have matters coming before parliament dealt with in such a way that there will be this information which will assist the electors who take an interest in what is being done by those who represent them, in forming their opinions as to whether the party that happens to be in office merits the confidence of the electors and should remain there, or whether, when the next election comes along, it should be replaced by others who might attempt to do better.
I think this explains why it is inevitable that there should be much more protracted debates in this house than there are in the other house. Nevertheless everything of a legislative character has to be considered and has to be passed by both houses of parliament. And I have never heard any serious complaint from any source that the members of the other house of parliament do not give consideration and study to legislation-which could not become legislation unless it had their concurrence. Because of the different atmosphere, the character and the democratic responsibility of that chamber, it does not take them as long to do their legislative work as it takes us here. But they have to do it. And there is no way under this constitution

whereby anything can become legislation until it has been approved and passed by the members in the other house.
Now, is that a good constitution? I must confess I have never felt that it was realistic to give any serious study or thought to the probability of modifying it. In order to modify it there would have to be also the concurrence of the members of the other house.
Since I have been in Ottawa I have found that there were plenty of problems that it was realistic to study and consider, because I might have some responsibility in connection with forming some opinions as to the solutions they should receive. I must confess I have never felt I was going to have in my day the responsibility of having to come to a conclusion about substantial modification as to the character of our constitution.
I have heard certain modifications suggested about the way in which appointments or summonses to the other house might be made. But quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I have never heard one that did not seem to me to bristle with more obstacles than promises of advantage to the Canadian public.

I thank you. I wish to be careful, and my intention was to deal with the principle of the bill, which provides that the same indemnity will be available for both houses of parliament, and not only for members in this house. And it is only in respect of that principle that I have ventured to make these remarks about the other place. When we adopt any measure in this house we do so because we think it is the right kind of measure to be adopted. We do not adopt it for the purpose of having it vetoed in the other house, where it has to be also considered and passed if it is to become legislation. It is because we think it is appropriate at this time to recommend these increases in indemnities that we have recommended them in the form in which they will apply to both houses of parliament and not to only one.
Now, I defer to your warning, sir, and I shall not say anything more upon that subject, but pass to the third point I wish to say something about, namely, the fact that in our view this is something which has to be dealt
Senate and House of Commons with by the members of parliament not in respect of their own individual interests but with the desire to do what they think is best for the vitality, proper development and proper maintenance of our parliamentary institutions.
I know that there are some hon. members who honestly believe that nothing is required to be done for that consideration. I believe it is the members of parliament themselves who are in the best position to know just exactly what the situation has been over the years with respect to the duties, obligations and possibilities of a member of parliament maintaining decent living conditions for himself and his dependents, with the length of sessions that cannot be very much shorter if we are to continue to regard this as the principal forum from which come the inspirations to the electors of the country for their proper conduct when they have to exercise their right at election time.
We may differ, as was said earlier today, but I think we all believe that each and every one of us is endeavouring to discharge his duties to the Canadian people to the best of his ability. It is in that light that hon. members should approach this question, and those who feel, as some honestly do, that no increase in indemnity is required, and any increased indemnity would be wrong, will oppose the legislation. But there are those who feel that an increase is proper and that it would be better for the future of these democratic institutions to have a situation where one does not really have to be fairly well off in order to be able to assume the responsibility of representing his fellow citizens, if he is the kind of person his fellow citizens think would make a proper representative for them in parliament. It is with that view and because I think that the future will amply justify the validity and the usefulness to the Canadian people of what is being recommended in this bill that I submit it for the consideration of my fellow members.

Mr. Speaker, I concede that the problem is one of some considerable difficulty, and I agree with the Prime Minister that it is not an easy one to deal with, no matter when the subject may arise, nor how it may be dealt with.
I agree with many of the observations he has made in regard to the necessity for adequate sessional allowances to make it possible for those who would make good members of parliament to offer themselves as candidates whenever the election may come.
The Prime Minister spoke of the fact that there were some who did not think there
1640	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons should be any increase in sessional allowances. I may have missed some statement that was made, but I do not recall a single statement made along that line. I have been under the impression that there has been general agreement that there should be an increase in the sessional allowances paid to members of the House of Commons.
As the Prime Minister has said, the members of the House of Commons know from their own experience something of the financial and other burdens imposed upon them in respect to the responsibility of representing their constituencies wherever the constituency may be. I had thought there was general agreement that it is appropriate that there be an increase of sessional allowances to members of the House of Commons which will make it possible for those who would make good members to offer themselves, regardless of their personal financial position.
Having said that, I then point out that we are in a position which is not different from that which has existed on other occasions and in other jurisdictions when it was regarded as wise to examine the situation and consider the alternatives and to establish some figure based upon due consideration and exchange of ideas and the participation of other members from other parts of the house in the deliberations leading up to such a decision. May I point out that in this case, as is its right the government has presented to parliament a measure, or in fact two measures, dealing with extensive increases, and that has been done without any examination of which we are aware which would tell us where those figures came from.
I could not agree more about any subject that might come up for consideration in this house or discussion in this house than I do with the words of the Prime Minister when he said that we should follow the course which will assure the effectiveness, efficiency and vigour of parliament, and that in arriving at conclusions in regard to the measure now before us we should have in mind the dignity of parliament itself, and the opportunity that is afforded, by the measure of allowances made available by statute, for the very best type of men and women to come here as members. With that I agree wholeheartedly. That still does not absolve us from the responsibility for arriving at these decisions by orderly methods and applying the same tests as we would apply to any other case where substantial changes were being made and where we were asked to adopt certain figures having considerable importance in themselves to any substantial segment of the Canadian community.


It seems to me that the demand for that type of information and that type of inquiry is far more exacting when our own interests are concerned. If we wish parliament to have that measure of respect which is in itself an essential factor in maintaining our system of government in these troubled days, then it is not only a case of getting the right type of candidate, it is also a case of being sure that members of parliament follow a course which will commend itself to the public when their own personal interests are concerned.
For that reason I still feel that it is extremely important that by one method or another there should be inquiry which shows us in some way the digesting processes by which a certain figure came out at the end. These figures were not simply grabbed off a rack; these figures must have come from some consideration of some kind. We have simply put forward the thought that in a matter of this importance the process should be very carefully designed.
The Prime Minister has said something that I think might well be taken as a guide by a number of his supporters in parliament. When some of them become impatient, as they listen to speeches made on this side when there is before the house some measure which they are anxious to have adopted, I would commend to them the rereading of the Prime Minister's words of a few moments ago when he said that all of us will admit that many speeches are made more for information of the public than for the effect the speech is likely to have in the house.
I doubt if there is any statement that the Prime Minister could make in this house with which I will agree more completely. Of course there are times when we are encouraged to hope that even in the house speeches may have some effect. There was the recent occasion when the minister for northern development with great courtesy very generously explained the reason for introducing an amendment to a bill which he had placed before the house as a government bill. That was a welcome sign. If any hon. members opposite noticed an increase in the amount of debate that followed, perhaps in some degree they must blame the minister for northern development for encouraging the belief that speeches do sometimes have an effect in this house.
We have had still further encouragement today. A few days ago we raised some question about the automatic application of the increase in sessional allowances to the pensions act. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) asked the Prime Minister if he would give the undertaking that legislation

would be introduced to limit the application of that change in its operation on the pensions act. The Prime Minister was quite emphatic in saying that he could give no such undertaking. In the meantime the arguments put forth-at least I hope this is the case-have had some effect, and today we have had introduced in this house and given first reading a measure dealing with this aspect of the problem. So I would say that we have had some encouragement.
Nevertheless, I think the general proposition is correct and in large measure remarks might be directed toward the information of the public. But I still hope that remarks may also be given some consideration here in the house.
The Prime Minister has given various reasons for proceeding in the manner in which he has. He has told us that there are three points which have guided the government in presenting the legislation in this way. He has explained that it is only rarely that members deal with indemnities or allowances and that whatever decision is made should be one that will extend over a considerable number of years and be adequate to avoid the necessity of coming back here too frequently for further revision.
Then the Prime Minister also dealt with the question as to why the government did not think there should be discrimination between indemnities in the house and the Senate. He explained that he considered that this is related to our constitution. He pointed out that at the time this country became one under the British North America Act the constitution had provided for two houses.
I think most of us, perhaps not all, will agree with that system, no matter how much we may disagree with the position in which it now finds itself. The Prime Minister may well say that the people of Canada have been given the opportunity to reform the Senate in some other way. I was not aware, when the party of which he is a distinguished member, many years ago and frequently since then, promised to reform the Senate, that this was the type of reform they proposed. He has stated that he has never seriously considered the practical possibility of those kinds of amendments to the constitution which would bring about a change of this kind. He has felt that there was plenty to do in this house without embarking on that difficult course.
I can only say that this must sound strange to those who for so many years promised Senate reform. Nevertheless we have the statement of the Prime Minister today that no such reform is now contemplated by the
Senate and House of Commons Liberal party. Obviously the present method is to continue. I do not intend to extend my remarks for fear of challenging the ruling of the Speaker already made as to the possible consequence of that course. Nevertheless this is one subject that the Prime Minister has placed before us and one that we cannot disregard.
We know that it is a delicate subject. We know that it is one that has to be dealt with having full regard for the dignity of parliament, which embraces both houses and the members of both houses. When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) tells us the same amount has always been allowed to the Senate and the House of Commons may I point out, without in any way reflecting upon the members of the Senate or the dignity of that house, which is an essential part of this bicameral system which came to us under our constitution, that the considerations that have been placed before us justifying an increase in allowance to the members of parliament do not apply to the members of the Senate.
I am not prepared to say there should be no increase to the Senate. It is conceivable that there may be arguments which would justify an increase in the allowance to the members of the Senate to the same amount as that paid to the members of this house. But, Mr. Speaker, if there is such an argument it has not been presented, and if there are any facts to justify that conclusion they have not been placed before us.
We were told, and I think we will agree with the proposition, that one of the reasons it is essential that there be a reconsideration of this subject at this time is the great increase in the cost of living, and above all, the increased time that members must spend in Ottawa, or at least most members. The Prime Minister pointed to the fact that it is expensive for members to keep in touch with their constituents, and in that he is entirely correct. He is also correct when he points out that this is not a task that is measured by attendance here in the house, and that an effective member of parliament is constantly in touch with his constituents interpreting their requirements and informing himself in regard to what is taking place, as well as doing a multitude of things in regard to the services of one kind and another which are offered by the government.
Then there is the subject that can be perfectly frankly discussed, and that is the cost of elections themselves. That has been indicated as a reason why we should have regard for the position in which members find themselves. In fact, some hon. members might almost smile-I perhaps should

Senate and House of Commons not put in the word "almost"-if they went back and read that on an earlier occasion when there was an increase, the optimistic prediction was made that election funds would no longer be necessary because the amount that was to be paid in the House of Commons would fully cover all expenses of that kind. That argument, of course, has not been made during this debate, but it was made in this house.
Whatever reasons there may be, Mr. Speaker, for increasing the allowances to members of the House of Commons, not one of those applies to members of the Senate. They are not elected, so they have no election expenses-that is, no local election expenses. They have no necessity for that measure of contact with their constituents which is referred to by the Prime Minister as an essential consideration in keeping themselves informed, nor have they as lengthy a stay here in Ottawa, nor are these stays broken by the legitimate and proper demands on members of the House of Commons to address various meetings and maintain these contacts that are essentially a proper part of our political system. If we are looking for reasons we will find they are reasons outside of any put forward to support the increase for the members of the house.
The Prime Minister made a point of the fact that he was glad we had adopted a similar form of parliament to that at Westminster, and he did that in discussing the need for an increase for the members of the Senate. Well, Mr. Speaker, with all deference I must say that I find it very difficult to follow that argument, because we do not borrow our methods in this regard from Westminster. At Westminster the lords in the second chamber do not get anything, so certainly we did not get the idea of having the same amount paid in the House of Commons as in the upper chamber from Westminster.
Whatever may have been true in days gone by, when the increases were relatively small,
I do not believe that would apply today when the increase can only be regarded as substantial. The Prime Minister gave us the history of the various allowances that had been made, and gave us the years in which increases had been made. But hon. members will realize that from 1867 the increases were relatively small on each occasion until 1920, when the largest increase was made. It was then $1,500. Now we have the proposed increase of $4,000. That figure may be right, but I would point out that a commission in

Senate and House of Commons
On an earlier occasion I put forward my belief that the dignity of parliament, which the Prime Minister has emphasized, and the respect of our people for our parliament and the way it conducts its business would be increased by an assurance that we had applied the strictest tests to any measure or measures that would benefit us in any way. The Prime Minister has replied to these proposals very frankly and has dealt with the suggestion that we should have a royal commission or a select committee. He has seen fit not to adopt that suggestion.
In view of that fact I am unable to support the bill. The principle of the bill is not merely an increase in salaries. If that were so, then we might just as well say that we believe in everybody getting more money, outside of this house as well as inside. There is more than that. The principle involved in the bill now before us cannot be divorced from the way in which the changes have been arrived at and the result that is to be produced. There are many cases where details may not be satisfactory but it may be entirely proper to support a bill on second reading, particularly when there is going to be a further examination, as in the case of a bill before the house just a few days ago which was being sent to the banking and commerce committee. There are a number of cases where it is obvious that it is appropriate to criticize, to examine, and try to amend.
In this case, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the bill, as it stands, cannot be divorced from the inadequacy of the procedure by which it comes before us. I think we must have regard also to the principle that, when our interests are involved, the most precise method of arriving at the figures must be followed. This principle is not met by this measure. I propose, therefore, to vote against this bill. I propose to do so without any suggestion that there should not be an appropriate adjustment of allowances in keeping with established figures and facts, but because there should not be just an accumulation of figures put before us without any explanation as to how they were arrived at.

Then it was said that the indemnity should be increased because of the many handouts we have to make by way of wedding presents, presents at christenings, wreaths at times of funerals, as well as many other things. I am in the very happy position where I am not asked for such handouts. My constituents know that I am not a wealthy man and that I cannot afford such largesse. Their weddings, their christenings and their funerals they can look after themselves. I am quite satisfied that that should be the case, because in my opinion these things are too intimate for a member of parliament to interfere with.
As I said, I am not saying that no increase whatever is justified; and at the proper time this party will make known its views in the matter. But as I have said, I do not believe an increase to the extent of 100 per cent is opportune at this time. Hardly a worse time could have been found for putting it forward. What do we find? In employer-employee relationships the employers are adopting a "hold-the-line" policy. That is a refusal to make any wage increases. Unemployment is increasing alarmingly all over the country. I am sure every member is receiving letters from his constituents about this. Prices of farm commodities are falling. All around us wages, salaries and incomes of all kinds are falling; and just at this moment the government introduces a measure of this kind that, as I have already said, increases the indemnity of members of parliament by 100 per cent or, if we include the expense allowance, by 66g per cent. It is at times like these that people look to their representatives for help.
As I said before, every hon. member is receiving requests from old age pensioners, persons on war veterans allowances and from persons on small incomes and superannuation pensions that were given by this government at a time when our dollar was worth very much more than it is today. To every such request made there is just the one answer, no. Then to add insult to injury we raise our own indemnities by 100 per cent.
I tell this house that this can have only one result; it will lessen public confidence in our

parliamentary institutions. Perhaps I can do no better than read a sentence from another letter I received the other day from Oak Bay. Westerners will know where Oak Bay is. It is a wealthy suburb of the city of Victoria. The writer of the letter signs his name T. Fox-Decent. This is the part I wish to quote:
The shameful example of grah, and the callous indifference to the plight of the burnt-out and old age pensioners, and the blind, . . .
Commons votes billions to combat communism but is indifferent to the fact that this constant grabbing for themselves will swell the ranks of communism by many thousands.
There is no doubt in the world, if we read the press and if we take heed of the letters we get, that there is strong resentment in the hearts and the minds of the people who are being neglected while we are looking after ourselves so generously.
As I mentioned in my remarks at the resolution stage of this measure, I am opposed to increases to members of parliament and members of the other place, because they tend to separate the public representatives from the people whom they represent. I am afraid it is not recognized by members of this house that with our present income we are already in the high-income bracket. I hold in my hand the taxation statistics of the Department of National Revenue for the year 1951. It is entitled "Taxation Statistics 1953," but the figures are for 1951. With our present indemnity, members of parliament are already receiving incomes higher than 89-3 per cent of those paying income tax or making income tax returns. If the increases proposed go into effect members of parliament will be among the top 1 per cent of income receivers in Canada. I am afraid that position will make things rather difficult for some people. It is my contention that people so far removed from the trials and struggles of the average individual cannot feel those trials and struggles and will not work to remove them.
The history of all nations demonstrates that improvement never comes that way. The dynamic strength for improving social conditions has always come from the bottom and not from the top. For the benefit of my Liberal friends I should like to quote a saying by the late William Ewart Gladstone many years ago:
I painfully reflect that in almost every political conflict of the last fifty years the leisured classes, the educated classes, the wealthy classes have been in the wrong. The common people-the toilers, the men of uncommon sense-these have been responsible for nearly all the social reform measures which the world accepts today.
If we are going to put ourselves among the top 1 per cent of income receivers in this

country we will come to fear changes because things are good for us as they are. The poor get very little thought now, but they will get less then because we will not feel any of the discomforts that the poor feel.
I have not much more to say, Mr. Speaker. I want to quote from an editorial in another Vancouver paper, the Province, which appeared long before this proposal came before parliament. The Vancouver Province is a paper which has a reputation for conservatism with a small "c". For that reason we should pay some attention to it. The editorial commented on some remarks I made when I spoke on the debate on the address, and said:
British Columbia probably has, proportionately, more of these people than any other part of Canada-
That is, more old age pensioners.
-because of our mild climate. In Vancouver many live in poorly-heated bedrooms, attic rooms and improvised basement suites.
I want the house to note this:
They seldom have enough proper food. Never do they have enough for the small luxuries that make life worth living.
I challenge any member of parliament here to say that he goes to bed hungry at night and that he is denied the small comforts that, as this paper says, make life worth living. But I tell you that in the city of Vancouver thousands go to bed hungry every night, and they have nothing left to buy these little comforts which make life worth living.

In order to be helpful, and I do try to be helpful, I warned the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) before he read a letter that if he did read it he should disclose its source. I gathered that perhaps he did not understand fully my intervention. In order to assure him that I did not interrupt him without reason I should like to refer him to citation 265 of Beau-chesne's third edition which reads:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.
Then citation 270 of Beauchesne's third edition reads:
An unsigned letter should not be read in the house.
The citation then goes on to give instances where the Speaker suggested that such letters should not be read into Hansard, and I quote:
Such a letter should not be read into Hansard; all letters when read must be signed and they become part of the documents of the house.
I should like to explain what I consider to be an unsigned letter. If an hon. member reads a letter and does not disclose its source, it appears in Hansard with no source being divulged. In my opinion that is tantamount to being an unsigned or anonymous letter, and such letters must not be read. The hon. member will perhaps recall the two occasions

Senate and House of Commons on which I can place my finger at the present moment when my predecessor, Mr. Speaker Macdonald, ruled in identical terms. I would refer the hon. member to Hansard of December 19, 1951. On that day the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Dinsdale) was speaking and the leader of the C.C.F. party inquired whether there was a ruling that required private letters to be identified. Mr. Speaker Macdonald then said, and I quote from page 2210 of Hansard:
I am not requiring the hon. member to disclose the source of the two letters he has just read. If that was to be done, I should have requested it earlier. However, if he intends to read other letters, he should disclose their source.
Another occasion was on November 28, 1949. The incident at that time was one with which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) may be familiar, because he was the one who was called upon to divulge the source of the letter.
I should like to make it clear that this is the reason I warned the hon. member. It may be that when an hon. member is warned before he starts to quote a letter he may decide that if he has to divulge the source he will not quote the letter. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this matter which is now before us is one on which every member of the House of Commons should take his own stand. I would not like to think that this was a party matter in any respect, and for that reason I hope hon.
fMr. Speaker.]

members will be prepared to make their stand known, as I certainly shall.
I was not able to be here last Tuesday when the resolution was discussed, and as a consequence I did not have a chance to express my opinion on the principle of the resolution. But my colleague, the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) did so on behalf of our group, and I concur fully in what he said.
The principle of the bill now before the house is to provide increases in the indemnities and allowances to members of the House of Commons and certain salary revisions for officers of the two houses and cabinet ministers. With that principle I am in agreement and I have my reasons for being in agreement. I look upon this whole matter, not as a measure to increase the personal income which members of parliament may enjoy, but as a measure to make it possible for every member of parliament to be a better member and to serve his country and his people as they expect to be served. That is the way I look upon this bill.
I am afraid there has been too much inclination in some quarters to consider that we were simply meeting here at this time to vote ourselves an emolument that would put us into a preferred class. That is not so. I am perfectly satisfied that any increase in the indemnities of members of parliament will be reflected in better service to the people of this country. I am satisfied that that money will be spent by members in trying to serve the people who sent them here.
With that as a background I would like to deal briefly with some of the things said by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis). It seemed to me that the whole burden of the speech given this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition was that we had been shown no justification for the figures which are presented in the bill. "What justification is there?" said the Leader of the Opposition. Well, I should think, Mr. Speaker, no one would be in a better position to answer that than the Leader of the Opposition. Statistics are the best justification I know, and he ought to be familiar with statistics for he has quoted them often enough in this house. Anyone who examines the statistics of the time, who has made any study whatsoever of increases in costs and prices since 1945, ought to realize that since that time there has been no less than a 100 per cent increase in salaries and wages generally over the country, and from 100 to 150 per cent, and more in many cases, in prices. What more justification does anyone want?

The Leader of the Opposition must know that when it is necessary for a member of parliament to visit his constituency today he is out of pocket two or perhaps three times more than formerly. For example, let him buy an automobile-not be furnished with one-and he will find that he is paying just about twice what he would have paid in 1945 and before, and he will buy one today that will hardly withstand the shocks of the road as the old one did. You can almost put your fist through one today, whereas formerly the steel gave some protection to a man. Let him buy gas and oil to visit his constituency and get around there; let him pay for his meals or transportation by train and all these things, and he will find that costs have increased by twice and in many cases more since 1945. I would think the one thing to do is to take a good look at the statistics, and he would have ample justification.
The Leader of the Opposition also referred to what happened in the United States. They did appoint a commission, as the hon. member is suggesting in this case, and that commission investigated, heard evidence, and brought down recommendations. But these recommendations went far beyond what the Prime Minister and the cabinet have decided here.
I think the Leader of the Opposition should have pointed out to the house how moderate was the position taken by the Prime Minister in the introduction of this bill. If we had had a royal commission to investigate and seek justification for certain figures, it is quite possible that such royal commission would have brought down a recommendation similar to the figures presented by the commission in the United States. Perhaps that is what the Leader of the Opposition seeks. I am not saying that, but at any rate it appears to me that we have some guide for our actions here when we reflect that in the United States it was decided to increase sessional allowances to members of congress to $25,000 a year, plus certain perquisites which I think bring the total up to something around $41,000.

The members of the House of Commons ought to have assistance in research. They ought to have made available to them means by which they can get the facts and figures with respect to the problems that
Senate and House of Commons come before them in order that they may put forward sensible solutions, based upon facts instead of fancy. We have tried to get that introduced in this house, but the principle has never been adopted.

speechtext:
In the United States that principle has not only been recognized but adopted, and the practice has been followed for many years; I think it was adopted as long as eight or ten years ago; certainly for as long as I have been in this house. I believe congressmen are granted something like $10,000 a year with which to secure assistance for research work. As a consequence one would expect the debate and discussions to be on a higher plane, as it would be here if members of the House of Commons had a similar allowance. We have not had the means with which to carry out this research, and I am afraid that as a consequence some of our debates have suffered.
There is this to be said also, that you cannot expect members of the House of Commons to serve their constituents as they wish to be served and still be their own research assistants on $6,000 a year. It is quite impossible when you stop to consider the increasing needs of the members from year to year. In a growing and more complicated society such as Canada, $10,000 a year will not go very far and will not more than make it possible for members of this house to enjoy a reasonable standard of living and at the same time discharge their responsibilities. Anyone who has given the slightest consideration to the facts and the statistics would never ask that question, "Where is the justification?"
When the Prime Minister said to me, as he did, "We have given this whole question of increased sessional allowances deep and earnest consideration, and we have decided to bring in a measure to make certain changes;" and then when he had the courtesy to outline what the changes were, I took it for granted that he meant that he and his colleagues had given the matter study. I believe he did.
I know this matter has been talked of around the corridors of this house for at least two years that I know of, and perhaps more; and I feel certain, knowing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) as I do, that he and his treasury board would never consent to increased sessional allowances without giving the whole matter the most earnest consideration. I have seen his work before, and I have every respect for the manner in which
1650	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons he discharges his duties. Anyone who stands up in this house and says there has been no consideration, no basis on which to decide how much the increase should be, is, I believe, stretching it a little bit too far.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that I need to deal with that part of it any further. I recognize that there is a difference between the Senate and the House of Commons. Certainly there is a difference in the responsibilities attaching to each. I do not know, though, whether this is a proper occasion to speak of Senate reform. I will not. I will simply say this. Perhaps the Senate ought to be reformed; but, Mr. Speaker, it certainly ought not to be reformed by an annex to a bill of this kind.
That is all I am going to say. If the other place is to be made the useful body that I believe it can be under our system, then certainly the way to go at it is not the way we have been going at it here since this measure came before us. I believe there is lots of room for improvement, and maybe the government will pull something out of the hat before the twenty-second parliament is completed that will help make the other place the useful instrument that it can be in a democracy.
I have never been one to suggest that the Senate be abolished, because I believe there is a place for a bicameral legislature in Canada. I believe it is useful, and I think it is unwise for us to enter too freely into a discussion of the comparative merits of the two houses of parliament. But I will say that certainly senators have no elections to fight, and as a consequence they are not out of pocket as members of the House of Commons are. Certainly the expenses of senators are nothing like those of members of the House of Commons, and certainly it must be conceded that the Senate indemnity-I am not speaking of the senators but of the Senate indemnity-is in the nature of a pension. We have to consider that. It is in the nature of a pension, and because that is so maybe there is some difference. Maybe there should be a considerable difference between it and the sessional indemnity of a member of the House of Commons. I am not going to make that an issue; I am merely pointing it out.
On the other hand, members of the House of Commons work barehanded. They work very hard to dig out facts and figures to keep themselves informed, and I believe everyone in the country must recognize that they do a pretty fair job, carrying on as they do without staff. I say it is not possible for members of the house to do effective work


without research, and I hope the government will give consideration to the introduction of some kind of research assistance for every member so he can discharge his duties and discharge them well.
Let me point out that originally the sessional indemnity for the House of Commons was based on a five-year term. In principle that is what we have now, but everybody knows that in recent years no government has dared to go the full five years. Consequently we have had an election every four years, which has made it necessary for members to go to the country and spend their money more often than they did in the days when there was really a five-year parliament. That is something that should be considered and that many people do not think about.
Then there is another point. Many members of the house, perhaps most of them, now consider that the work of a member of parliament is a full-time job. I know it has been with me. Since I came into this house it has been impossible for me to spend any time whatsoever in trying to supplement the income I have had from the House of Commons. There must be a good many hon. members in the same position. Consequently what they receive by way of indemnity has to cover their living expenses plus the cost of their service to the public, and that of course often means maintaining two home establishments. I say to hon. members that this is not commonly known, that it is a consideration, and a big one.
As I listen to people outside of the house talking about things, I gather that they believe that the work of a member is over when a session ends, and that all hon. members have to do is go home, bask in the sun for the rest of the summer and fall, go hunting and fishing and what not, and wait until another call comes to return to the house. That of course is the greatest of errors. The work of a member of parliament does not end when a session of the house closes, and that must be kept in mind. He really has to start on his hard work then. He has to get around a very large area and pay his own expenses while doing so. If he does not visit his constituents in every part of his riding, report to them, talk to them, help them to open fairs and start drives of one kind and another during the period between sessions, he is not considered to be doing his duty.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the demands on members of parliament are very great, and I am not prepared to say that members are not entitled to an indemnity of $10,000 with

which to discharge their responsibilities. I certainly would not be in a position to make any such claim. I say that adequate pay to members of parliament, whatever that adequate pay may be, would make it possible for members of parliament to give their constituencies the kind of service that is required in a democracy. Let me go a step further and say something that I believe can be proved to be the case. I think an adequate sessional allowance for members of the house would be one of the greatest inducements toward better service because there would be keener competition for the job of member of parliament. That would force present members to extend themselves in giving service. There is no question about that, and if the people want good service I am satisfied that they are prepared to pay for it.
Let me come now for a moment to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis). He quoted some letters. As the leader of a party, Mr. Speaker, I have received but two letters. In the past two weeks I have had fifty times more letters about a flag than I have had with respect to the sessional indemnity. As the leader of a party I imagine that I would receive quite a number of letters if there was widespread dissatisfaction throughout the country with what parliament is doing.
I have been trying to keep my ears and eyes open, but as I say, I have received only two letters. One of them was strongly critical and the other simply said, "under the circumstances, do you not think you ought to be improving the lot of the old age pensioners and the recipients of war veterans allowances?" That is all.
Maybe the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway draws all these letters. Maybe he has received more than I have. Maybe Vancouver is a place where people feel more strongly about these things. I am giving him every benefit of the doubt, but I do not believe for one moment that the number of letters members are receiving can be very great. Otherwise I am sure my group would have received their fair share, and they have not so reported to me. In 1945 I listened to an almost identical speech made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. He made the same dire predictions he made today; not a bit of difference in the world. He told us at that time that he would vote against the $2,000 expense allowance because he was a socialist. Well, he took it just the same.
