He is still a socialist. He is going to vote against this measure. That is
Senate and House of Commons his privilege. I do not want any person to have to take something he does not want, and when the bill is in committee it may be possible to make some arrangement so that such people will not be embarrassed. Maybe it can be arranged that the increase over the $4,000 now paid will have to be applied for, a system of election, much the same as we had to do in the case of the pension. In that case we had to elect. Well, I am just giving a notice that I have a little amendment that will help the situation along when the bill goes to the committee. Then we shall see just how much of this talk is on principle and how much is for political purposes.
I sat here today and listened to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway make a few rather sly remarks about the Social Credit member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), and Social Credit governments. He was speaking about old age pensions, and that sort of thing. I want to remind him that for a good many years the Social Credit government of Alberta has been making a $10 supplementary allowance, above the $40 given by this government, to old age pensioners, while the socialist government of Saskatchewan has only been giving $2.50. If that is socialism'-well! I shall go further and say that the Social Credit government of British Columbia is doing the same as the Alberta government.
I am going to let matters stand, Mr. Speaker, by saying this. I look upon this as a measure designed to make it possible for the members of this parliament to give the people the kind of service that the people deserve and want. I stand in support of the principle of the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Measures such as this, Mr. Speaker, are always difficult to consider dispassionately in the house. In my remarks today I am not questioning the good faith of any member in any part of the house. I was unable to be here on Tuesday when the debate on the resolution took place, but in reading Hansard I thought the Prime Minister had ended his remarks with a very worth-while suggestion. These words are to be found on page 1454 of Hansard for January 26, 1954:
These matters should be dealt with exclusively on the ground that the opinion expressed by each individual member will be his opinion as to what will really in the long run serve the interests of the Canadian people whom members of parliament are here to represent.
Today I propose to follow his suggestion and give my opinion. Incidentally, earlier in the same paragraph the Prime Minister intimated to his own followers that they were free to vote on this measure as they

Senate and House of Commons saw fit, and that the life of the government would not be in jeopardy by reason of the vote. Those words were as follows:
I would say to hon. members on this side of the house that if they honestly believe these increases are not in the long run to be in the best interests of our democratic institutions, they should not feel that because I am the one recommending them at this time they should submit their judgment to mine.
I am very much disturbed, Mr. Speaker, about this plan because I believe, in the first place, that it will weaken the prestige of parliament. Some hon. members have argued it will increase the prestige. My personal opinion is that it will do the opposite.
I am disturbed also about it because I believe it will tend to bring into public life in Canada people who are more concerned about the salary than they are about the service they can render to their fellow Canadians.
I should like to place three considerations before my fellow members. The first is this. The election was fought about six months ago. The Canadian people were not told at that time of any plan to increase the indemnity. The Prime Minister in his speech the other day rather intimated that the people had been told the indemnity would be increased. Here is what he had to say, and it is found at page 1452 of Hansard for January 26, 1954:
My colleagues and I came to the conclusion that this problem should be tackled from two angles, and that was the reason why I stated in the national broadcast I made from Vancouver on July 9 of last year that it was our policy-
Then I go on to quote what he had to say in Vancouver, that part of his speech being in quotation marks in Hansard.
"to seek appropriate amendments to the rules of parliament with a view to ensuring speedier and more orderly conduct of the nation's business without any abridgement of the rights of the opposition or of any minority to give expression to its views. We believe that if men and women of ability are to continue to be attracted to public life some way must be found to reduce the length of some of the debates in parliament, and to make the conditions of membership less burdensome than they have become in recent years."
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, in that statement there was no direct reference to any increase in the indemnity. I presume the Prime Minister had that in mind when he uttered these words, "to make the conditions of membership less burdensome", but the ordinary person hearing that would think he was referring to the length of time the session lasted. If it was the intention of his party to increase the indemnity, then I think in fairness to the Canadian people a clearer statement to that effect should have been made. We get to this position, therefore,


that the members of this parliament stood for election, and were elected, on the basis of the present indemnity.
The second consideration is that the Prime Minister is now bringing in a proposal which, in effect, is to increase the indemnity 100 per cent. I admit that in one or two years there were two sessions which meant, of course, a double indemnity, but I think it is fair to say this proposal means an increase of 100 per cent in the indemnity. The expense allowance was introduced and passed by the house on the basis that it was to cover expenses, and that it was not to be considered in any way as pay; of course there was a difference between the House of Commons and the Senate in so far as the $2,000 was concerned, in that the allowance to the senators was made taxable.
I do not believe the Prime Minister has said anything today that constitutes a justification for an increase of 100 per cent. Perhaps there should be some increase; I am not disputing that. But from one coast of this country to the other this increase of 100 per cent in our indemnity will start demands for increases in pay. Within the next few weeks it will be used in dozens of bargaining negotiations. We have the hint also that our high court judges are to be the next to get increases in pay. They have had two increases within a very few years. The argument is being made now that because members are having their indemnity doubled there should be an increase for the justices of the high courts.
I do not believe an increase of 100 per cent can be justified at any time, under any conditions, and certainly not at this particular time. I believe that for several reasons. In the first place, Canada has moved into a high priced economy. We have had warnings from responsible men across this country within the last few weeks that that is the position in which we now find ourselves. We are having more and more trouble selling our goods abroad because we are having trouble competing with other nations. So I say this is a time when this nation is in considerable danger because she is getting into a high priced economy. For that reason this is no time for the House of Commons to be setting an example by doubling our own pay.
Then, this is a time when unemployment is a grave threat. I hope it will not become any more serious than it is at the present time, but from one coast to the other today unemployment is extremely serious.

There is one other reason which is close to my heart, and I hope I shall not be accused of using an emotional argument. If so, I cannot help that. However, I must say that the House of Commons has failed to take into consideration recommendations made unanimously in 1952 by a special committee on veterans affairs that the ceiling on the permissive income of recipients of war veterans allowance should be increased. This is not only a case of people outside the house asking for an amendment of that kind; it was a unanimous recommendation by the special committee on veterans affairs.
These men, the great majority of whom were front-line troops, are in the position that if, for example, they reach the age of 70 years, they cannot get the full benefit of the old age security payments, because when they take those payments their war veterans allowances are cut so that the total income will not be more than $60 a month. That situation should have been remedied long ago, and in my opinion should have priority over an increase at this time in our own indemnities. Many of these men are on a starvation basis. We have hundreds of them in British Columbia. On a basis of comparative population we have more war veterans allowance recipients in that province than in any other province in Canada. There is a crying need that their problem be met before ours is dealt with.
The third consideration is this. Obviously this proposed indemnity of $8,000 plus the $2,000 for expenses is meant as pay for a full-time job. There will be monthly payments of indemnity amounting to $666.66. In addition to that there is the tax-free expense allowance of $2,000. And yet, Mr. Speaker, this is not a full-time job. No matter what hon. members may argue to the contrary, I submit it is not a full-time job, and I have as my authority for that statement the Prime Minister himself. This is what he said, as reported at page 1452 of Hansard:
It was never intended, and it is not now intended, that members of parliament should be salaried servants of the state. Members of parliament are representatives-that is true of members of both houses of parliament-and, to be truly representative, it is desirable that they should be drawn from a wide variety of occupations and walks of life-
And I stress these words.
-and that they should be able to retain, while they are members of parliament, their connection with the occupation or walk of life and the area from which they were chosen to be representatives in parliament.
I could not agree with any statement more thoroughly than I do with that statement of the Prime Minister. I believe it goes to the root of the democratic system. Are we to
Senate and House of Commons have here representatives, or are we to be paid as civil servants? Then he said at a later point in his speech:
While membership in parliament should not be, and should not be regarded as being, a full-time occupation-
And so on. We must be in our constituencies at least half the year. Most of us are able to be, even those of us who represent constituencies on the west coast. When we are in our constituencies for that length of time, I do not know how a member could sit around and do nothing for six months. There is some political work to do, but there is opportunity for a person to earn at least something. And I think it is of great benefit to the member to get back into his own business and get right down among the people so that he may learn something about the problems they are meeting. I always consider it takes a lot of foolish ideas out of my head when I have to go back and do a little of my regular work. It is of great value that the members should resume their places in the life of the communities from which they come for at least a portion of the year. So let us not say that this $8,000 plus the $2,000 free of income tax is for a full year. It could be much more accurately described as payment for half or three-quarters of a year.
Then, Mr. Speaker, the doubling of the indemnity is bad enough in the case of members in the House of Commons, but this same increase for senators cannot in my opinion be justified on any ground whatsoever. As a matter of fact the Prime Minister made the argument this afternoon that they had to be treated the same. Well, they are not treated the same in the expense allowance. A difference is recognized right there. They pay income tax on their $2,000, but we do not.
I am afraid there enters into this picture the fact that the Senate has the veto on legislation passed by the House of Commons, and that they may say, "Here, we will not pass this bill at all until we get exactly the same as the members get". That is a situation that might as well be faced by hon. members of the House of Commons and by the Canadian people.
There are long periods when the house is sitting and the Senate is not. They rarely sit on Mondays or Fridays, even when they are here. And the amount of work done in the two houses, when both are in session, cannot be compared. For example, we have to deal with the estimates, but the Senate does not have any work of that kind.
Would you call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose for the dinner recess I had almost completed my remarks. If Your Honour will recall, at that time I was pointing out why I thought this doubling of the indemnity to the senators could not be justified on any grounds whatsoever. I had explained three of my reasons, and I should like to add one more. It is this. Unlike the members of the Commons, once the senators leave Ottawa their responsibilities end; for if they have any responsibilities out in the provinces it is very difficult to see what they are. They have no constituents; they have no elections to face. Their position in the constituencies is entirely different from that of the hon. members.
I do not criticize the senators as individuals. About one-third of the present Senate have served with me in the House of Commons, at one time or another, since 1935. I think they are all my friends, at least they were until today. I do not blame them individually; they are victims of a system.
At the present time all those in the Senate, with the exception of seven, are followers of the present Prime Minister. There are 15 or 16 vacancies, and I believe there have never been fewer than 12 vacancies since he became the Prime Minister of Canada. That fact in itself shows how little value he places on the Senate, and I am rather surprised that he can come into the house today and ask that they should be given the same increase as proposed for the members of the Commons. No Prime Minister has ever had a finer chance to do something about meeting the situation in the Senate; yet, instead of making any move to reform, our Prime Minister is doubling the indemnities of the senators.
For the reasons I have outlined I repeat that I believe this bill in its present form is unfair to the Canadian people. They are entitled to better leadership than is being given in this instance.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should take part in this debate, not because I think I can throw any new light on the subject but because I have been a strong advocate of better indemnities for members of parliament. I have been in this parliament for a good many years. In that period I have talked to a good many members of parliament about their financial problems. I have known men who saw their livelihood going to pieces, who have not been able to get along on their indemnities, and they had
IMr. Green.]

to go back to their professions or their businesses. I have known men in this parliament who have seen themselves getting deeper and deeper into debt without any real hope of improving their position. That is not a healthy situation.
I was an employer of men before I came here, and I always considered it my business, if I thought one of my people was getting into financial difficulty, to see him and find out what the trouble was and to help straighten out his affairs. I do not believe that people who are worrying about financial problems can do their best work in this House of Commons.
I think hon. members will accept the fact that I have no personal axe to grind in this debate. I was more fortunate than most hon. members in that I was able to practise my profession for 30 years before I came to this parliament. I was fortunate in having an earning power when there were no income taxes, and later when the income taxes were not heavy. I am old-fashioned enough to think that when we are earning we should save for our old age, and I did that. The result was that when I was invited to stand for this parliament in my fiftieth year I was able to assess the situation, as most people must do when they are asked to stand for parliament, and accept the invitation.
I think every man in Canada is attracted by the thought of serving his country in the parliament of Canada, but it has been my experience that a great number have had to say "no" simply because they could not see any possibility of making both ends meet. I know I have asked a number of people to stand for parliament. Any member of the government is interested in building up the strength of the party he represents.
I have had a good many people consider coming to this parliament, and many people, in fact the majority, have said: "I cannot see how I can support my family and do what you are asking me to do".
I think that most men, surveying the situation, view it in that way. I know I did.
I was willing to sacrifice my earning power- that was unimportant-provided that I did not have to sacrifice the standard of living of my wife and children. I think that is a reasonable attitude. I believe a man, when he marries and is raising a family, is under obligation to do the right thing by his family. If he has built up a standard of living for them I do not think he should take on any work that means a lowering of the standard of living or a lessening of the chances of a good education for his children.

I examined the situation in that way, back in 1935, and found that I could afford to stand for parliament. I have been very happy with the remuneration I have received since then, and I would be very happy to finish my term in this parliament with the same remuneration. That is the personal position. But I suggest to this parliament that personal views should not govern. After all, is not the problem this? We are fixing the remuneration for people from coast to coast, in order to arrive at an average that will bring to this parliament the kind of people that we should have in it. You say, "How do we determine that average?" Well, I think the people most capable of determining it are the people who have had experience in living the kind of life that members of parliament are required to live.
It has been said often that there are only two classes of people who can afford to stand for parliament; people who have considerable capital, and people with no money at all. It is a well-recognized fact that if a man comes in here with a small capital, a capital that would mean a great deal if he could go on accumulating, he is bound to dissipate that capital, not in extravagant living, but for purposes that are proper for those who occupy our positions.
I have heard an hon. member say that he is not called upon to make any expenditures in the constituency. Well it has not been my experience to have that kind of constituency; I do not think it has been the experience of many people in this parliament to have that kind of constituency. I would not want to operate that way in any constituency. When I lived in Port Arthur, before I entered this house, I tried to enter into the activities of the community, to support worthy causes, and I would not want to change my position in that regard just because the people of Port Arthur have sent me to represent them in this parliament. I do not think any of us want to change our ways completely to settle down to an isolated life, to not be able to take part in community activities or in the activities of the district we represent, just because we are in this parliament.
The question is this. What is a reasonable remuneration, on the average, to compensate hon. members for the loss of income they suffer in coming to this parliament? It was said by the hon. member who spoke before me that many members can use the summer months to supplement their incomes. I think that situation varies. Professional men can do that. In fact when I entered parliament that was one of the factors I took into account, that I would spend six months at Ottawa
Senate and House of Commons but would have another six months in which I could practise my profession. It so happened that I was taken into the cabinet before I entered the House of Commons and was not able to do that. Perhaps you may think that cabinet ministers are very well paid, but I would exchange what I get as a minister for the privilege of having that six months in which to practise my profession.
We are determining what indemnity will attract able men to parliament, the type of men that we think the various constituencies would wish to choose to represent them in parliament. As I say, his indemnity should compensate a man for the time he loses from his own work and for the cost of maintaining two domiciles, as many members must. I take the view that if a man has a wife and five children, as I had when I ran for parliament, he should not have to leave his family at home for six months in the year. His indemnity should be sufficient so that he can provide a home and thus enable them to live with him when he is here in Ottawa. Just to look at the statistics, the increase that is proposed now does not seem unreasonable. It has been said that we should not have an increase here in this parliament because other people have not had increases. I do not know of any class of people who are working for a living, people who are willing and able to work, who have not had an increase since 1945. Since 1945 the cost of living has increased about 60 per cent, and wages and salaries have increased much more than that in proportion.
We regard our work as important. We say that we carry the responsibility for government, and so we do. I suggest to you that no successful business that I know of believes that it can succeed by holding down the salaries of its executives below the point that enables them to live in a way their occupations entitle them to live. That is not considered good business outside this house, and in my opinion it is not good business inside this house.
The people in this house are in various circumstances. As I say, a professional man can supplement his earnings in the recess. The businessman very likely has an income that goes on whether he is in parliament or whether he is in his place of business. But there are a great number of members who are neither professional men nor businessmen. They have been chosen by their electors to represent them here, and it is not easy for many hon. members to get the supplementary income necessary to supplement what they receive here.

Senate and House of Commons
It has been said that we should go outside this house and appoint a royal commission to determine the proper scale of parliamentary indemnity. I do not know where we could get more information about the situation than from hon. members themselves, who are experiencing the situation we are trying to remedy. I am sure that if we had a royal commission made up of business people who were getting business salaries they would recommend indemnities which the government could not recommend to this parliament. I am sure that if we had a royal commission made up of people who earn less than we are proposing we would get recommendations that would be on the scale they found adequate to maintain themselves. In my opinion either finding would be meaningless.
No one outside of this house can appreciate the conditions under which members of parliament live and carry on their work. I am sure every member of the government has had conversations with a considerable number of members; and it seems to me, therefore, that the government is in position to recommend an indemnity which is proper under the present circumstances.
It may be that if we enact this legislation, some of us will not come back to the next parliament. I know there are a number of capable young men in Port Arthur constituency who would be likely to stand for my seat if they believed they could make both ends meet while doing it. I think they should have their opportunity. Just because I was able to live and earn in a rather exceptional period and they have to contend with present scales of taxation, I do not see why I should be the man to represent Port Arthur and they should be debarred from standing for office.
I daresay the same situation obtains in many constituencies, in that there are a number of able men who are not presently in a financial position to stand for office but who would be able to do so if this change in the indemnity is carried.
I think that is all to the good. I believe it tends to make for a better parliament. I believe the people of Canada will support the action we propose in this bill. I have had a good deal of experience with working on the prairies. There are many representatives from the prairies in this house. I worked there as a professional man for many years, and I never found the people of the prairies a bit reluctant to pay the salaries or compensation that the service justified. Incidentally the farm organizations pay as high salaries as any other business organization. I have never found any feeling of reluctance to pay for the service that was needed at the going rates.


I have had some experience with other classes of people. I notice that the representatives of labour here in parliament are not dissenting from this bill. Why? Labour believes in paying its officers and its representatives rates of remuneration that will allow them to live properly and carry out their functions adequately. I think that that is the real feeling of the people of Canada. They want good representation in this parliament and they are willing to pay a reasonable indemnity for that representation. Therefore I have no hesitation in supporting this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all of us in the house appreciate the moderate and dispassionate manner in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has just discussed this very important question. I want to say that I could not agree more with him than I do when he says that we should look at the issue on principle, not in terms of personal situations.
I may say further that I could not agree more than I do with the Prime Minister in the closing words of his remarks of last Tuesday. If I understood him correctly, he addressed those closing words primarily to the members on his own side of the house, but they might well have been directed to members in all parts of the house. I refer to his suggestion that members should make their own decision in respect to this matter in the light of what they feel to be best for our Canadian democratic institutions.
It is on that basis, Mr. Speaker, that I approach this question. I could do it on a personal basis. I could discuss my personal situation and that of others, but I do not propose to do so. Rather, I feel it is incumbent upon me, as I feel it is incumbent upon others, to answer this question:	What
is best for parliament? What is best for democracy? Is it a good thing for the Canadian parliament, for Canadian democracy, to provide for an indemnity and allowance to members of parliament totalling $10,000 a year?
I want to say right at the start and in as clear terms as I can that I do not believe it is good for parliament, for relations between this Canadian parliament and the people of this country, to pay that much and thereby create the economic difference that it will establish between members of parliament and the people whom we represent. I do not go to the other extreme. I do not suggest that it would be good for parliament to have the members of this house paid so little that they would be up against it all the time. That would be just as bad for

parliament as to pay an amount of such size that it separates us too far from the people we represent.
I said a moment ago I did not believe we should go to the other extreme and pay members of this house too little. On the other hand, bearing in mind some of the arguments that have been put forward from time to time during the course of this debate, I cannot help but note it is a matter of history that when the indemnity was only $600 a session-it is true that was a long time ago, and it cost a lot less to live in those days- the fact that the indemnity was only $600 did not fail to attract to the parliament of Canada such an outstanding person as Sir John A. Macdonald. I draw attention also to the fact that when the indemnity was only $1,000 a session it did not fail to attract to the parliament of Canada such persons as Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden. In the same vein-

speechtext:
My hon. friend knows far
better than that. Hon. members of this house know for a fact there have been many great Canadians across the years this parliament has been in existence who have come here because of their desire to serve the nation or because of certain principles for which they were crusading.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, if I may make a more modern reference, that I am thoroughly satisfied that when a certain gentleman by the name of Louis St. Laurent back in 1941 was approached to enter parliament, it was not the money which attracted him here at all. Neither was it the money which attracted a certain C. D. Howe back in 1935. My plea is that hon. members should not promote the idea that we have to have a sizeable indemnity in order to attract good men to parliament. The record of the Canadian parliament is a splendid one, and good men have been attracted to it across the years because of a desire to serve the nation, or because of a crusading spirit which has brought many outstanding men and women to this House of Commons.
I simply wanted to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that I do not believe we should pay too little, nor should we pay too much. It seems to me the problem that faces us is one of degree; one of finding an amount that 83276-105
Senate and House of Commons will make it possible for men to fill this position and carry out the duties of a member of parliament without having so much that they are too far removed from the ordinary people of this country.
It is all right to quote statistics about the rise in the cost of living; it is all right to quote statistics about the increase in the levels of wages and salaries, but everyone in this house knows that the great bulk of the people in this country today, both salaried people and wage earners, are in the bracket between $2,000 and $3,000 a year. Also bearing in mind, as so many hon. members have stressed, the large number of old age pensioners and people on war veterans allowances who are down in the economic cellar, I suggest we should consider seriously the distance $10,000 a year removes us from the people we represent. I think that amount is too much, for the good of the parliament of Canada.
My leader has already mentioned, and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway pointed out this afternoon, that we recognize that a case can be made for some increase over the amount which is provided in the statute at the present time. We will indicate again, as has already been done, what we think would be a reasonable amount when we go into committee on the bill, if the bill receives second reading. At this stage, when the government is proposing a total figure of $10,000 a year, most of us in this group believe-and we are all free in this group to have our views on this question-that it is not the best thing for the parliament of Canada and it is not the best thing for democracy to remove us that far from the great mass of the Canadian people by paying ourselves that much money. That is the reason we are voting against this bill.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister in his remarks today-and he, like the Minister of Trade and Commerce just now, dealt with the matter very dispassionately and in very moderate tones-did suggest that perhaps one of the reasons some hon. members voted against the resolution last Tuesday was that it was a package proposition. I think that is probably true with respect to the reason for the vote against the resolution on the part of some hon. members.
But may I draw to the Prime Minister's attention the fact that what we have before us in this present bill is still quite a package. There are still quite a number of items in it, so it is not just the one question of increasing our own indemnities in this house which is now before us; it also includes the same increase for the members of the other
1658	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons house of this parliament. In addition there is the provision for an increase in the salaries that are to be paid to various officials-the Leader of the Opposition in this house, the Leader of the Government and the Leader of the Opposition in the other house; the Speakers of both houses, and the Deputy Speaker of this house. I am not going to take time to deal with all these various increases; but I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that back in 1947 when it was first proposed that there be any salary at all for the Leader of the Government and the Leader of the Opposition in the Senate-in addition to their regular indemnities-we took very strong exception to that proposal and voted against it, and in taking that position we had the support of most if not all the members of the Progressive Conservative party and I believe most, if not all, the members of the Social Credit party at that time.
That is still our view. We feel that the total emoluments being paid to these gentlemen are adequate for the job they are doing, and that just because other increases are being provided-and they share in these other increases-there should not be these additional increases in their salaries as well.
So far as the Senate as a whole is concerned, my views on that question are so well known that I do not need to take much time to develop them at this point. I was a little surprised this afternoon when the Prime Minister said he was not concerned even about any modification of the Senate. I would not have been surprised if he had said he did not agree with those of us who favour abolition of the Senate, but he did not even use that word. He just referred to modifying or reforming the Senate in any way, and he said there were other matters which were of more immediate concern to him.
I am interested in the fact that no less a person than George V. Ferguson, who knows a good deal of what is going on in the Liberal party, in a book that he wrote a short while ago entitled "It's Our Business" had something to say about this matter. He said:
Nevertheless, Senate reform has been a plank of one or more Canadian political party platforms for more than thirty years. It made its appearance first in the Liberal platform of 1919, doubtless because the Liberals were looking forward to power and feared what a Conservative Senate might do to its legislation. The plank is still there, but nobody does anything about it.

speechtext:
I was merely quoting an *outsider to support my statement that it is the general belief in this country that the Liberal party has stood for Senate reform since 1919. We now find in the words of the Prime Minister today that what George Ferguson said is perfectly true. The plank is still there but nobody does anything about it. Apparently it is the intention of the Prime Minister not to do anything about it as long as he is Prime Minister.
But it does seem to me that at a time like this, when we are being asked to increase the -amount of money paid to those who serve in the other place, it is appropriate for some of us who feel strongly about it to say again that we believe there is no need in the Canadian parliament for a second house, particularly one as unrepresentative of the Canadian people as is the Canadian Senate. Therefore if we are opposed to a Senate at all, we are by virtue of that belief opposed to increasing the indemnities paid to members of the other place.
I draw the Prime Minister's attention to the fact that a great many people and a great many newspapers in this country who do not share our view that the Senate should be abolished are nevertheless shocked at the proposal to increase the indemnities of senators to the figure proposed in this legislation. I hope that even yet-I dared to hope it particularly this afternoon, when I thought the Prime Minister was not too sure of his case on this point-consideration will be given to leaving the indemnities paid to members of the other place where they are at the present time.
There are one or two other matters in connection with the bill before us about which I feel I should say a word. The Prime Minister has detailed the history of the Senate and House of Commons Act in respect of the changes that have been made from time to time in the indemnity. I have not gone back to 1867 to check the point about which I am now going to say a word, but I have checked back through two or three of the changes and I find that when the indemnity stood at $2,500 a session the provision with respect to the amount of money that a member would lose for lost time, that is absence in excess of 15 sitting days in a session, was $15 per day. When the indemnity was increased to $4,000 the figure of $15 per day was raised to $25. Again

in 1945, when the $2,000 expense allowance was added, it was provided that for every $25 lost in respect of the indemnity there would be a loss of $12.50 a day with respect to the expense allowance. In other words the total loss for days absent in excess of the 15 per session that are allowed was raised to $37.50 per day.
My point is that on each of the last few occasions when there has been a bill like this before the house amending the Senate and House of Commons Act for the purpose of increasing the amount paid to members, a corresponding increase was made in the amount to be deducted for days lost in excess of 15 per session. But I look in vain for any such change in the bill now before us. It seems to me that the Prime Minister should follow suit, and just as on each of the previous occasions to which I have referred the penalty for lost time was increased, so the penalty should now be increased.
The figures I have given, $15 per day when the indemnity was $2,500, $25 per day when the indemnity was $4,000, and $37.50 per day as it is now, are all roughly proportionate. They are not exactly the same. On the basis of the same proportion the amount should now be either $60 or $62.50 per day. I suggest that when we get into committee the Prime Minister should consider putting another section in the bill to change the appropriate section of the Senate and House of Commons Act that deals with the question of lost time.
I may say that I believe the government should go a great deal further. I think the whole question of attendance in the house should be reviewed, perhaps by a committee of the house, and some more satisfactory means should be found of keeping a record of the attendance of members and of making sure that indemnities are not drawn unless members really perform the service for which they are elected to the House of Commons.
As a matter of fact there are two or three other changes of that kind that it seems to me should be made at a time like this, but I shall leave them until we get into committee on this bill or on the bill that is to follow amending the Salaries Act. The Prime Minister no doubt knows some of the things I have in mind. I have before me a memorandum prepared some years ago by Mr. Watson Sellar, the auditor general. The whole point I am making is that things that need to be tidied up in the Senate and House of Commons Act and in the Salaries Act do not get attended to in the periods between the major changes that are made. Therefore 83276-1051
Senate and House of Commons now is the time to make changes with respect to these ancillary matters, or we all know they will not be made at all.
I shall not take the time of the house to deal with details of that kind now but will do so when the appropriate time comes. In the meantime I hope that hon. members generally throughout the house will agree with the Prime Minister, with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and with me that it is up to each one of us to make our decision with respect to the bill now before us on the basis of what we think to be best for parliament, best for our democratic institutions, and best for the relationship between us and the people of Canada whom we were elected to represent. On that basis I shall vote against the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise and make my position quite clear on this matter. Stated quite simply, it is that I am not in favour of any increase as suggested in the bill.
I might say that the right hon. Prime Minister did a fair thing, and should be highly commended for the manner in which he introduced this bill. He should be commended particularly for the statement he made at the conclusion of his remarks. What I have to say and the position I take on this matter do not and should not, I think, reflect on any member in this house. I believe it is our responsibility to come to our own conclusions, in conformity with what the Prime Minister said during his introduction of this bill.
I should like to read that to the house, as reported on page 1454 of Hansard of January 26, 1954:
I would say to hon. members on this side of the house that if they honestly believe these increases are not in the long run to be in the best interests of our democratic institutions, they should not feel that because I am the one recommending them at this time they should submit their judgment to mine. These matters should be dealt with exclusively on the ground that the opinion expressed by each individual member will be his opinion as to what will really in the long run serve the interests of the Canadian people whom members of parliament are here to represent.
I heartily agree with the sentiments expressed by the Prime Minister, and it is entirely on that basis that I have come to the conclusion not to support any increase at this time. I know that every hon. member

Senate and House of Commons in the house will readily agree with me when I say that there are members in this house who are here for no other purpose than public service. This is certainly true in the case of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), as well as other members. We do know that in the introduction of this bill they have no personal axe to grind. They are doing it because they believe it is in the interests of parliament and the country that such a bill should be passed at this time.
I think I can speak with some degree of authority on my own position at least, because I am not a new member in the house, having represented the old constituency of Assiniboia from 1945 to 1949. I appreciate the difficulties, of course, that some of us have to face in being members of this parliament. I accepted the nomination as a great honour. At that time I was a registered Canadian seed grower and a producer of registered Hereford cattle. Having a specialized farm, 1 know some of the things that can happen "to a member when he spends 75 per cent or more of his time in the business of representing his people. I do appreciate the financial position of some hon. members.
Again in the last election the people came and persuaded me to accept the nomination to represent them. I accepted it knowing full well that there might be financial considerations and perhaps certain sacrifices to make. I did this, sir, without any knowledge whatever of any intention on the part of the government to increase the indemnity. At this time I do not know what my constituents would think, except that I have had statements from one or two against accepting any increase. It is on my own responsibility, however, after giving great consideration to the matter, that I have decided not to vote for it.
In the first instance, this party is on record as being against the Senate. This in no way reflects on the members of the other place. I know some of those members personally, and I know that they are honourable members. We just do not believe the Senate is a necessary component of parliament, and it costs the Canadian taxpayer well over a million dollars a year. I do not consider it in the best interests of parliament to increase their sessional indemnity.
I want to say that when coming down here I felt there were a great many things that should be done. We still have these recipients of war veterans allowance; we still have our old age pensioners; we still have our superannuated civil servants, who by no stretch of the imagination can be said to be receiving fair treatment from the Canadian government.
(Mr. McCullough (Moose Mountain).]

Then I should like to refer to the statement made just before the dinner recess by the leader of the Social Credit party, who said it would be very easy to determine the increase necessary for members of parliament on the basis of statistics. This may be true, but I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he said he did not think it was in the best interests of parliament that members of parliament should be too far removed from the people of Canada.
I have a sessional return dated January 29, 1954, which contains the answers to certain questions concerning the incomes of our Canadian people. According to this paper there are 452,427 who earn less than $500; 443,140 who earn between $500 and $999; 601,652 who earn between $1,000 and $1,499; 690,792 who earn between $1,500 and $1,999. In other words, there are 750,889 wage earners who, according to the latest statistics I can find for 1951, earned between $2,000 and $2,499.
Another figure which I have here, Mr. Speaker, shows what sort of bracket hon. members of the House of Commons will be in if the increase is granted. I find that, according to taxation statistics, 1953, from the Department of National Revenue, which outline the position for the 1951 taxation year, there were only 1 [DOT] 2 per cent of the Canadian people earning $10,000 or more.
So far as I am concerned, I cannot favour the increase. I do not think it would be in the interests of the people. There are some other things which should be done, which I have mentioned, before we would be in a position to support this measure.
In conclusion I might say that if I needed any further argument to encourage me to vote against this measure, I received a letter just the other day from my wife. I had written her saying that there was some movement on foot to increase our indemnity. In her reply she said that I was sent to Ottawa to represent the people and get something better for our farmers who were caught in the price squeeze today. She did mention the old age pensioners, too. I believe, Mr. Speaker, on that ground I must take the position I have outlined.

speechtext:
I am going to try to explain that, and whether or not I shall be successful the hon. member may judge. There have been many good reasons given for raising the indemnity, and I shall mention only one; it was mentioned earlier this evening by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That is the fact that we often fail to get the kind of candidates we want because they just feel they cannot come here, with the indemnity as it is. That is, I think, a very good reason for being in favour of it, and I am in favour of it.
But my vote is a protest vote. It is a protest against the manner in which this has been carried out. I submit that if this had been carried out properly there might have been no need of my being in the position I am in now.
I wish to compare this situation with one or two other things that have been done. In this case the government, for reasons I do not understand, seems to have behaved in a manner entirely different from that which it adopted when the pensions were introduced. At the time of the pensions there was a consultation with the different parties before the measure was brought to the house. We had a chance of making our contribution, for whatever it was worth. Then there was a committee which studied the matter for a long time, and a great many things were brought to the attention of that committee.
While I admit that pensions are in a somewhat special category, and while I admit that in the long run we do have to be the judges of this thing-because there can be no other final judges-I do submit that by setting up a committee we would be in a better position to reach the conclusion we have to reach. I wish to support what I am saying by pointing out that in a similar situation in Great Britain-entirely similar, so far as I can see -they did appoint a committee; and I wish to read briefly from British Hansard of May 29, 1946, quoting from a speech of Mr. Dalton, who said at page 1233, 5th series, 1946:
We felt it would be very much better for a committee of the members of the house to look into the
Senate and House of Commons question quite frankly without any direct lead from the government as to what was desirable. Therefore, on 15th November last a select committee was appointed, and it issued its report on 6th March. On 30th April, with the authority of the cabinet, I made a statement in the house of the government's proposals, which in substance and on the great majority of points at issue, follow the recommendations of the select committee.
We are very grateful to the select committee for their work, and I am glad that the report of the select committee was unanimous. Upon the select committee there served some members of considerable experience of the house, and also some young members who brought to the discussions the freshness which is appropriate to new arrivals, and between them they agreed on a number of proposals.
I feel that the Canadian people were entitled to a better method of having this done. I feel that if this is passed without any committee being set up-because I do not think the committee of the whole house is the: place to have the kind of intimate discussion* we need in this instance-and if this is passed without any further means afforded for study and consideration, then when I go back to my constituency I shall be in a very awkward position. I shall be asked, "You increased your indemnity?" "Yes". "To $10,000?" "Yes". "On what basis did you do it?"-and. I feel that I may be in a very awkward position, because I really just have to say, "I don't know." At the moment we are in the position of the children who play that game: "Take any number; double it; divide by two", etc. I do not know how these figures are arrived at. I feel that we should have an opportunity to do what we did-and with good effect, I thought-at the time of the pensions.
There are one or two other points I wish to make before taking my seat. This has been said already, but I think I must repeat that it is in the highest degree unfortunate that this increase was never mentioned until recently. And I wish to draw attention ta what was done in 1945, at the time the expense allowance was given. I quote from page 3414 of Hansard, from the speech of Mr. Mackenzie King, where he said:
I had not intended to speak on the resolution but since others have made some comments perhaps I should say a word as to the obligation I have felt in the matter of introducing this resolution. I speak now more particularly to hon. members who have come into the house since the last session, the last parliament in fact. Hon. members who were present at that time will remember that before the end of the session I stated that X thought the allowance paid to members of parliament was wholly inadequate, having regard to their increased obligations, the changed situation in the world, and the corresponding enlargement of their duties since the allowance had been previously fixed.
I think it was unfortunate that that was not done in this instance. It is unfortunate that there was no consultation with other

Senate and House of Commons parties. It is unfortunate that this matter is brought in on a take it or leave it basis and that no committee has been set up, following what seemed to be a sound and wise course taken two years ago.
For that reason, though unwillingly, I shall vote against second reading; though I still hope, even at this late hour, that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) may see his way clear to follow the procedure of two years ago and let us have a committee. Because I repeat, it seems to me that the Canadian people are entitled to have this matter dealt with in a better way than is being done on this occasion.
Let me say again I fully realize the truth of what has been said, that in the last analysis we have to be the judges. But in my opinion the last analysis ought not to be until we have done the best we can to inform ourselves, that is, by considering what has been done elsewhere, so that we may have in ourselves-what I have not at the moment

a knowledge of the facts so that I can go to my constituents and justify the particular figures that are decided on.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not take up much time in this debate, because I have spoken on the matter already. At that time I gave my reasons for being in favour of the bill we are now studying.
I prefer being in favour everywhere I go, instead of being in the position of some members in the house who speak for, when behind the curtain, and speak against when they are in the chamber. I am not going to mention anyone, but I am just making this observation so hon. members will know that I am not talking one way outside the house and another way inside.
I listened with great interest this afternoon to the Leader of the Opposition, who said that while there might be reasons members in this chamber should be entitled to an increase, he did not feel the same applied to members of the Senate. He placed some figures on record in which he showed that members of congress in the United States were receiving $27,000, although it is proposed that we receive only $10,000 here. He said it would be hard for us to explain why we give the same treatment to senators as that given to members of the House of Commons.
In the city of Montreal the council is composed of three classes, namely class A, class B and class C. Class A councillors represent the landlords; class B represent the non-proprietors, and class C represent the people sent to council by different organizations. I believe there are 11 of them,
[Mr. Macdonnell.l

among others the board of trade, the chamber of commerce, the University of Montreal, and other organizations of the like.
All three different classes of councillors are given the same treatment. However, the class C councillors are not elected by the people, but are named to council by their own organizations. In the class C group, if one is a member of the executive committee he will receive $7,000 a year, just the same as any other member of the executive who must be elected. Indeed, we find that the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton) is in class C, in the city of Montreal; and as such he is paid the same amount that is paid to the members who are elected by the people. If anybody thought that we were creating a precedent by giving people who are not elected the same indemnity as people who are elected, then may I say here is a good example. A city of a million and a half people has given the same treatment to non-elected representatives as they gave to the elected representatives.
I shall take my seat after this. I just wanted to give the reasons why I shall support the policy of giving an increase to the Senate. This afternoon reference was made to the poor people, to the people who are on old age pensions, to those receiving blind allowances and all those other social allowances that we give. Well, if for one moment I thought-and I say this because I represent a constituency composed of working class people to the extent of 80 per cent-they would be harmed by the action we are taking here or would be deprived of having more done for them, then I would be the first one to oppose the measure.
I shall not use the word I used the other day, Mr. Speaker; I was told we must not use that kind of language, but it is not right to say that we have no use for the poor people or that we do not care for them because we are giving ourselves an increase. If you took your pencil you would not have to calculate very long to arrive at what this will cost the people of this country. It will cost every citizen of this country about ten cents a year to give fair treatment to their representatives.
I do not know if there is anybody in this parliament who does not need an increase. I would be inclined to vote for an amendment of the nature suggested by the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low) when he spoke this afternoon. If any hon. members feel that they do not need the increase there may be an opportunity for them to say whether they want the increase or do not.

Senate and House of Commons
So far as I am personally concerned I am not ashamed to say that after my experience I wonder if I can afford for long the luxury of being a representative of this chamber at the indemnity we are receiving now, namely $6,000 a year. In my last speech I gave the reasons for that. Without hesitation I say I know the mentality of my people, and I am sure they would certainly understand why their representative in this parliament has not been afraid to take his responsibility and give fair treatment to parliamentary representatives, not only for himself, not only for this parliament but for those who will succeed us.
Before taking my seat I want to say that if I thought the action we take here would mean that the poor people would have to endure worse treatment or more hardship than they are going through now, I would be the first one to oppose the measure.

I am very glad, Mr. Speaker, to withdraw that implication. I am sure the hon. member for Peace River would agree with me that if there is any man in this house who would refuse to abandon his convictions for political considerations that man is the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. He has proved that time and time again.
I was sorry to hear the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned money, say, "That is what you come here for". I would suggest that if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre were sitting on the other side of the house no remarks of that sort would be made about him. I fancy that the hon. members on the
other side would rather welcome the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on that side of the house if he could be persuaded to cross this floor, a contingency which I would say is not apt to happen. With respect to his ability or his earning power, if anyone wishes to sneer at the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as one of those who has come to parliament in order to make his living, I would say that a just-minded man on the opposite side of the house, including the Minister of Finance whom I have heard express himself in this regard, would be the first to say that there is nothing in that.
Since I am speaking of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, may I say that he often puts us on this side of the house in a rather unfortunate position, particularly if we have to speak after him, because when he has finished he has said in as precise a manner as can be just about everything that can be said. I had jotted down an occasional note which I wished to develop myself, but I find myself in the position that he has developed those jottings much more adequately than I could have done it myself. Therefore my object in rising tonight is simply to put myself on record as being totally opposed to this bill.
My reasons for taking this position are of course several. The Senate has been mentioned. I cannot see how anyone can consistently vote for an increase in the salaries of a group of men, no matter how excellent these men may be personally-and they are excellent men; I am not criticizing them at all-when he has spoken time and again in favour of that body's total abolition.
There is one thing, and perhaps it is the only thing new that I may mention, and I think it is fair to draw it to the attention of the house. While the indemnity at the present moment is $4,000 on a sessional basis, owing to the fact that it is on a sessional basis and owing to the fact that during the last parliament of four years there were two special sessions, that gave the members of parliament an extra $8,000. If that is spread over four years we find that an extra $2,000 a year has been received-I almost allowed myself to use the words "take-home pay", which is language that I deplore.
What it amounts to is this, that over the last four years each hon. member has received not $4,000 but actually $6,000. If the Prime Minister's bill had proposed an increase in the indemnity from $4,000 to $6,000 I should have found myself in support of that, not because it constitutes an actual increase, since it would not be an actual increase, but because it would simolv out

Senate and House of Commons upon an annual and a secure basis which one could expect to receive each year the amount of money which hon. members have been receiving over the last four years.
I think perhaps that would have been more reasonable. I could have voted for it, but I am not prepared to vote for an increase in the indemnity to $8,000. I can see the point that is raised that this would not give an actual increase of $4,000 but that it is really an increase of $2,000 in the amount that each hon. member would receive.
I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway expound the theory of economic determinism. I do not agree with some of my hon. friend's statements, but I do agree with that. I believe all of us, whether we know it or whether we do not know it, are influenced in our thinking by our own economic position. I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has a point when he says that if our own position is too far removed from the economic position of the vast majority of those whom we represent, we might not have the same understanding or sympathy for those who are less well off than ourselves. I believe that point is well taken.
I know that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) and many of my hon. friends who are older members on all sides of this house would not be so influenced. But I believe there is a danger in the indemnity or total take, if I may call it that, which is now proposed, in that we might attract to this house a group of people who were very interested in that higher indemnity; young men who have not had the opportunity, as some of us older people have, of suffering some of the hardships which many of us did during the thirties. I consider that the most valuable education I ever received, either at school, at university or anywhere else, was the one winter when I spent a total of $18 on my keep, a total which was supplemented by the rabbits I was able to catch in the woods. It is not an experience that I would recommend to my hon. friends except as a source of education.
I said I was not going to mention personal things, but perhaps hon. members will excuse that little personal story. I do believe there is something in the theory of economic determinism in that we have to suffer, we have to experience, we have to live, and not always in a sphere of life far removed from the troubles of the people whom we were sent here to represent.
I do not think anyone is going to be accused of being purely political during this
[Mr. Knight.)

debate. I know I am not going to criticize any hon. members or their opinions. We have all been sent here because our constituents thought it was a good thing to send us here. I am sure that whatever our indemnity may be we will continue to serve this country and the people who sent us here to the best of our ability. I shall vote against this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is only one reason I rise tonight and that is because my neighbour to the south, the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough), spoke before the last speaker. There have been a number of angles raised in this debate, but there is one point that strikes me and I shall come to it directly because we have not very much time.
Considerable emphasis has been laid upon pensioners and people who get only $2,000 or $3,000 a year, and it has been contended that before we do anything in this house with regard to raising the indemnity we should consider them. I give credit to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway for lofty motives in what he has said.
There is one point which has not been mentioned during this debate. There is another class of people ranging from Victoria to St. John's, Newfoundland, who spend billions, not just millions, upon beer, wine and whisky. In Saskatchewan last year $40 million was spent on liquor. The hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis) has said that this increase in the indemnity will represent only ten cents for every person in Canada. That is just one glass of beer.
Let us get a proper perspective of this bill. When any nation can spend that amount of money upon liquor-I am not saying anything against it because we have had this sort of thing going on since the time of Noah when the ark got stuck on Mount Ararat and they celebrated for three days-when any nation considers the liquor industry as being worth more to the people than its House of Commons, then there is something wrong with the perspective of the nation.
We are called upon to do a great many things in our constituencies as members. If we are going to fulfil our duties properly we should have the wherewithal with which to do it. This is going to help us a little; not altogether, but a little. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) is increasing his hardware empire throughout the entire area of western Canada, and he probably does not need it.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that at this hour any hon. member who is opposing this legislation is not likely to win friends or influence people, but I feel that the point of view which I propose to advance should be expressed. I do not mind admitting that I make mistakes from time to time. When I was here in 1945, when the last increase was proposed, I supported it. I have been sorry since that I did not stand by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway in opposing it.
I think there may be very good reasons for giving members of parliament some allowance for expenses, but that increase came at a time when we had successfully held the price line through some very critical years. Every organization in the country was pressing for increases in prices. They wanted to increase the price of steel, the price of farm implements and so on. Workers wanted increases in their wages. What was a perfectly legitimate piece of legislation to make provision for expenses was understood by the people of this country to be an increase of 50 per cent in our indemnity. There was a tremendous reaction against that throughout the country, and by the time things settled down we realized that $6,000 was not any better than $4,000.
On this question I believe our public relations have not been too good. As recently as a week ago a well-known writer, John A. Stevenson, in his "Ottawa Letter" published in Saturday Night not only made some critical remarks about the $2,000, but gave us an extra $1,000. I must admit I have never been able to locate it. He mentions reduced rates for staying at the Chateau Laurier; mentions that we get a very good meal in the parliamentary restaurant for $1, and that we do not have to pay our stenographers. As a farmer I was never required to hire a stenographer. My wife never charged me $1 per meal, and I find that though the 83276-108
Senate and House of Commons Chateau Laurier gives a reduced rate of $5.50, there is not one of the 23 members of this group who takes advantage of it.

speechtext:
I think it is unfortunate that a well-known correspondent such as Mr. Stevenson, who has the advantage of many privileges in this house, should write in that fashion. His paper is the only one I know of which sends a canvasser around from room to room in this house to secure subscriptions for this paper. He has made three visits to my room without obtaining a subscription, and he does not even ask whether or not it is convenient for me to see him. I suggest a paper that takes that sort of advantage of the good nature of the members here should not accuse us of getting $1,000 which none of us ever get.
Before returning to the House of Commons I was one of those fortunate farmers who was in the happy position of being able to pay income tax. I say that sincerely, because I am sure more farmers are worried about not having to pay income tax than about paying income tax. I found when I made out my returns that I was entitled to include expenses. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) supplied us with a very helpful book wherein he gave the financial statement of an unnamed farmer who had a total income of $9,906, but he had expenses of $6,714. It makes a good deal of difference if you take these expenses into account before paying your income tax. If you paid income tax on that gross amount you would have to pay $1,952, but if you took your expenses into account you would pay only $201. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that members of all political parties have expenses which should be taken into account before paying income tax. However, that is water under the bridge.
Less than six months ago there were 900 candidates in Canada who wanted to come here very badly, but only 265 came. In my constituency there were five candidates, and I am sure if I decided tonight I could not continue to represent the people of Mackenzie for the present amount of $6,000 a year any one of the four would be glad to take my position.

Senate and House of Commons
The Leader of the Opposition did not make quite clear whether he wanted the sort of commission which investigated congressional indemnities in the United States. On investigation I found that their commission took five months to consider the kind of complicated question we are apparently going to settle in the next day or two. The commission issued a report with some interesting comments. They said the average congressman spends $3,000 a year more than his $12,500 salary; that many congressmen have to return to private life after a few years to recoup. However, they recommended an increase in the salaries of congressmen and district judges from the figure of $12,500 to $27,500. The Leader of the Opposition said that our two countries are somewhat similar, and that the cost of living is similar in both countries. But he did not finish up the point and say whether he considered the United States recommendations to be fair or unreasonable.
I for one have made some inquiries as to how members are treated in different countries around the world, and apparently there are a great many unreasonable demands on congressmen in the United States. I considered the position in the United Kingdom, New Zealand, Sweden, France and the United States. In the United States members are paid $12,500, but there is rent for office accommodation in your constituency; you are allowed 12,000 words for telegrams, and 30 hours in long distance telephone service from Washington to anywhere in the United States. Many services like that bring the total to up around $40,000.
However, I cannot help but remind myself, as a member of the C.C.F. party, that if I lived in the United States I could not be a member of congress. It is almost impossible for a member of a third party in that enlightened country to ever get a seat in congress or the Senate. At any rate, it has not happened for a long time and apparently it is not going to happen in the foreseeable future. In the other countries mentioned members of parliament, prime ministers and cabinet ministers receive much less than in Canada.
I appreciate the point emphasized by hon. members on all sides of the house regarding the contribution the present Prime Minister has made. I am told the return we gave him for coming here was probably less than a third of the amount he enjoyed as an outstanding lawyer. But there have been compensations. The Prime Minister is about to embark on a world tour. I believe there are men in Canada who would give a million dollars if they could exchange places with the Prime Minister just long enough to make this tour around the world. But a million


dollars will not buy that sort of experience; and the Prime Minister did not wait to come here before interesting himself in public service and endeavouring to serve his fellow men. What I said of the Prime Minister could be said of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I am sure of all members of the cabinet. I am proud of the fact that although the salaries paid to cabinet ministers during the war years were very small compared with the returns that went to some of the people doing business with cabinet ministers, we did not have any scandal in Canada during that period. Such a scandal would have weakened faith in democracy, and I am glad members of the opposition have not been able to uncover any scandal of any great proportion in connection with Canada's war effort.
I do not care whether I am accused of being a hypocrite by some hon. members opposite. I am prepared to let the people of Mackenzie decide that question. I want to suggest that life is a bit too short to place ourselves in the position that this move is going to place us in. In my opinion the net effect is not going to be nearly as attractive as some of those who are voting for this measure think.
I know the advice I gave to some of my friends on all sides of the house when I was here before was not taken too seriously. I suggested they go back home and get some of their supporters to put some money into their political party every year. The Liberal party, the Conservative party, the Social Credit party and the C.C.F. party-that is the only one I worried about-would all do much better if every person would select some party and support that party as generously as his financial position permitted.
I am in the happy position of having been a candidate on five occasions. I was elected three times and twice defeated, but on every occasion there were at least dozens of people in my constituency who put up more money for election expenses than I did. The net cost for me was very little whether we won or lost. I would prefer to continue my relations with my people on the basis that as a member of parliament I was not in as favourable a position as some of them have been who have operated farms or businesses during these more lucrative years.
I must also say that I do not see how in this day and age we can support an increase for the members of the other place. Surely a cheque of $500 a month for life for people who do as little as the members of the other place-I do not wish to reflect on any of them personally; many of them are friends of mine, although they probably will not be

now-is quite an ample amount, and the proposal to increase their pay by $333 a month is something I cannot support.
Then there is a final point that is important to me. I represent a constituency that has within it a very large number of people unable to pay any income tax. When I spoke on housing the other night I gave figures as to the value of housing in my constituency in 1941. I doubt that there is any constituency in the country with a lower average value for housing. I simply cannot go back to my people and say that I could not get along on $6,000 a year and had to have an increase. Therefore my position will be that I cannot support any increase.

If the Senate had a majority of Conservative members today I wonder if those members of the Conservative party in the house who have spoken would use the same tone they have used in this debate. If there were a majority of C.C.F. members in the Senate I wonder if C.C.F. members of the house would use the same tone they have used in this debate. I am very doubtful that they would. Because there is a Liberal majority in the Senate they have taken advantage of that fact to speak as they have, but I feel quite sure in my own mind, although I have no way of proving it, that if things were reversed they would adopt a different attitude.
Another thought I have in my mind is that this legislation was perhaps designed to keep the good members we have in the house. Let me say at the outset that I do not class myself as a good member. I would say that the legislation was designed to keep the good members and at the same time induce more able and efficient businessmen to enter public life. In the back of my mind there is the thought that some members of the house may be worried about the results of the next conventions. From the discussion that has taken place here it would seem that they fear there may be a little more competition when the next election rolls around. I for one am convinced in my own mind that, with ihe indemnity increased to $10,000, I will Shave to fight to get the nomination in my sown riding.
