Comparisons are made in the house as to prices, wages and a hundred other different things. We usually make use of the conduct of the socialists for purposes of comparison. The member who


spoke before me mentioned the indemnity paid to congressmen in the United States. Surely he is convinced that they are receiving a much greater indemnity than we are. He mentioned some of the services with which they are provided by way of supplementing their indemnity. Again this is something we do not have in this house. There is no comparison between the indemnity that is paid to United States congressmen and that received by members of this house.
Another fact that has never been brought to light in this debate is that if a member- I speak now for myself-receives the increase of $4,000 his income tax will be increased by anywhere from $1,600 to $2,000. That is as close as I can calculate it at the moment, but perhaps the minister could help me with the calculation. This would give me an indemnity of about $6,400. I believe that if you took all the members of the House of Commons and the members of the Senate and calculated what they would pay in income tax, you would find that instead of $10,000 they would receive a whole lot less. When the income tax is deducted it goes back into the government pot, so it is not $10,000 the people of this country will be paying to each member of parliament and each member of the-Senate.
In 1S05 the indemnity received by members of parliament was $2,500. In 1920 this indemnity was increased to $4,000 by a Conservative government. I believe you will all agree with me that in 1920 conditions were not too good. I can remember that year very well, and conditions were not good; but the Conservative government saw fit to increase the indemnity from $2,500 to $4,000. If the figures I am about to give are not correct, I should be glad to have them corrected. I believe that prior to 1939 the average total revenue of this country was about $600 million; that is what this parliament had to deal with. It has grown until today the revenue is over $4 billion. In other words you have seven times the revenue to deal with today that you had even 15 years ago. Surely that means longer hours and more work for members of parliament.
I should like to speak for a moment now about my own case, and then I shall resume my seat. When I was nominated in 1945 I was working for the civil service. At the age of 65 I could have taken superannuation which would have provided for my family and myself. I came here in 1945, and I have been here nearly nine years. If I were defeated in the next election, I would be over 50 years of age. No one in industry today wants to employ a man 50 years of age or over. The only hope I might have of finding

employment would be through the sympathy of a friend, and that is exactly the position in which I would be placed.

A night watchman might be a very good description of the position. I can assure you that since I came here nine years ago I have been able to get by, but I have had to live very carefully. I do not believe the citizens of the county I represent want me to live that way.
Hon. members who have spoken previously in opposition to this legislation have given me the impression that they are placing price tags upon themselves. I have no quarrel with that, but I do not want them to put a price tag on me. If anyone is going to put a price tag on me I want the electors of the county of Charlotte to do that. When the next election rolls around they will have an opportunity to decide if I am worth $10,000 or whether they would rather have someone else represent them.
Those are my views. I feel that the majority of the members in this house will support the increase in the indemnity before this debate is finished. There may be some who will change their minds and support this legislation. Again I want to say that if there is any member here who does not want to accept the increase, I do not believe he will be forced to do so. If he is happy with the $6,000 he is receiving, and is sincere in what he has said in this debate, I believe the Red Cross or some other charity would be happy to receive the $4,000 he does not need. I can use it, and I am going to support the legislation.
If I have said anything during this debate to leave the implication that members have not been sincere, those statements were based on the facts I have produced. It would appear to me that these members are willing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars for everyone else. We all agree there are more civil servants than there are members of parliament; there are more old age pensioners and there are more receiving family allowances, so it would appear to me as though they might be playing politics with this measure.
Mr. J. W. Nose worthy (York South):
Previous speakers have already referred to the fact that this is a package bill, and package bills are generally difficult to deal with. It is always a question whether we shall support the bill because of the sections in it which we can support, or whether we shall vote against it because there are sections in it which we cannot support. I believe we had an excellent example of that in the
Senate and House of Commons housing bill upon which we voted last week. There were a great many members in this house who criticized sections of that bill, but all of them voted in favour of it on the assumption that they should vote for that part of the bill which they could support rather than against it because of the parts to which they were opposed.
I believe we have to decide how we are going to vote on this bill. I do not think we can escape that responsibility by suggesting that we hand over the decision to some outside group. The Leader of the Opposition seemed to feel it was necessary to set up a royal commission to discover whether the Leader of the Opposition in this parliament should be paid $15,000 in addition to his sessional indemnity. I certainly do not need a royal commission to decide whether my indemnity should remain at $6,000 or whether it should be raised to $8,000 or $10,000. I fail to see: why 265 members of parliament should require a royal commission to enable them to decide what their indemnity should be.
I am going to support this bill, notwithstanding the fact that there are some things in it of which I do not entirely approve. I cannot support the increase proposed for senators, since the party to which I belong and to whose policy I subscribe is pledged to the abolition of the Senate. The only advantage I can see for the interests of Canada in the proposal to increase the sessional indemnity of senators is that it may hasten the day when the country will demand the abolition of that institution. I presume that if we were to pass this bill providing an increase in indemnity for members of parliament but no increase for the members of the Senate, the bill might be sent back to us. I am not sure that would not be a good thing. I think it would do a good deal to arouse public opinion in support of the idea which this party has supported.
I am supporting the bill in so far as increases for members of the House of Commons are concerned. I am supporting it on the ground that I have every reason to believe my constituents feel I am worth as much in the House of Commons, as a member of parliament, as I would be back in my own constituency, in the classroom of a collegiate. The position I vacated to come here in 1942: now pays a salary of $8,000 a year. That $8,000 would be worth much more to me as a teacher in that school than the $10,000 will be to me as a member of the House of Commons.
I think most of us are agreed that it is in the best interests of Canada, that, since parliament legislates for all classes of Canadians, all classes of Canadians should be represented

Senate and House of Commons in it. I am not satisfied that it would be in the best interests of Canada that we should have a House of Commons made up of 265 members from any particular class in Canada, whether it be industrial workers, farmers, or any professional or business group. Of course if there is any one profession that would be entitled to send 265 members here, and to provide a good parliament, that profession would be the teaching profession.
Since in a sense every Canadian is 'a shareholder in this parliament, I think it is in the best interests of Canada1 that all classes of citizens should be represented. If all classes are to be represented, then there are some to whom this must of necessity be a full-time job. To name only one profession, no school teacher in this country could undertake to come to Ottawa as a member of parliament and at the same time maintain connections with his profession. For him it must become a full-time job. I doubt whether any labour man working at his trade or in a shop could come here as a member of parliament and retain his former job. It must be for a labour man, as it has become for my hon. friend from Vancouver-Kings-way, a full-time job; and the indemnity must take that into consideration.
It is unquestionably advantageous that those who come here from business, from the professions or from the farms should be able to maintain contact with their businesses, their professions or their farms. I think there is an argument that members of parliament who belong to those groups can keep themselves better informed and in closer touch with the problems of those whom they represent by so doing.
However, I do not agree with those who maintain that the length of our sessions or

the number of times we are called together should be determined by the class of private businesses or professions in which those particular members are engaged. I am convinced that every member who comes here should make his position as a member of parliament his primary job, his most important job, his first job; and that any association he may have with his profession, business or farm should take second place to his position as a member of parliament. Consequently he should be available for any sitting, no matter how long, if the business of parliament requires that he be here for that length of time. He should be in a position to be here *as often as the business of the country requires.
Taking that into consideration, I can well understand how those who come here from business, the professions or even from the farms make a considerable sacrifice. I can well understand that if we are to have successful professional men, businessmen and outstanding farmers to serve as members of parliament, then of necessity we must be prepared to pay an indemnity that will help to make up for any sacrifice they may have to make.
On motion of Mr. Noseworthy the debate was adjourned.

maintopic: COMMONWEALTH FINANCE MINISTERS' CONFERENCE SYDNEY - JANUARY, 1954 COMMUNIQUE

speechtext:
We have met as the financial representatives of the United Kingdom, including its colonial territories, Canada, Australia, South Africa, New Zealand, India, Pakistan, Ceylon and the new Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
We represent not only peoples and governments devoted to the full spiritual life of the individual, but also between us, the greatest mass of resources, developed or potential, in the world.
We have discussed many matters of supreme financial and economic importance. We have carried on the work of the London conferences, reviewing the policies we then adopted and reporting to each other the progress made under those policies. We have been informed of the discussions between the United Kingdom, representing us, and the western European nations, and the United States of America. The relevant facts have been faced and future trends estimated. We have envisaged the development of our commonwealth, and have found ourselves confident of its strength and sure of its high destiny. The matters which we have to report may seem prosaic. But we ourselves have seen in them great possibilities and widening vistas for our own countries, for the commonwealth of nations, and for the world.
Great edifices must be built upon solid foundations, patiently constructed. We do not expect the complete building in a few months; but we have met in a spirit of self-reliance and of determination that success will be achieved.
In that spirit, we look with friendship at the other great nations, and invite them to be our collaborators in problems which may appear technical, but which are in reality the common problems of peace and prosperity.
We now state the considerations which we have had in mind, and the conclusions which we have reached.
1. The object of our present meeting was
to consolidate the economic progress made by
the sterling area and the commonwealth during the last twelve months to seek means to accelerate that progress and to ensure that they make their full contribution to world prosperity.
2.	During the last year the sterling area countries of the commonwealth have made great strides towards the objectives which they set for themselves in January, 1952, and confirmed and amplified in December,
1952.	The commonwealth countries rejected then, and we reject now, the view that any solution of our problems can be found in the creation of a closed system of discriminatory arrangements, which could lead only to chronic restrictions and recurring crises. We therefore reaffirm our agreed objectives, which are to strengthen the position of each country and of sterling as a currency, and to establish with other countries a wider and freer system of trade and finance in which convertibility of sterling is an essential part. Thus we shall serve the best interests of all, not only in our own countries but in the world as a whole.
The Outlook for World Trade
3.	We have considered the outlook for world trade. The commonwealth is responsible for about one-third of that trade. We are conscious of the vital importance which the actions and policies of our countries could have when, as must be the case from time to time, there is some uncertainty about the future.
4.	Our first resolve is to ensure that our own actions and policies will be such as to inspire confidence. We stand prepared to take appropriate steps, both individually and in concert with each other, to sustain production and trade and the sound development of resources, and to ensure that temporary economic fluctuations are not permitted to interfere with our progress towards our longterm objectives. We are also ready to cooperate with other countries and international institutions to this end.

Commonwealth Finance Conference
5.	In this co-operation the United States of America and Europe have a special part to play because, with the commonwealth and sterling area, they are responsible for three-quarters of world trade.
6.	We were therefore encouraged by the recent message from President Eisenhower to the United States congress in which he said:
This administration is determined to keep our economy strong and to keep it growing.
At this moment, we are in transition from a wartime to a peacetime economy. I am confident that we can complete this transition without serious interruption in our economic growth. But we shall not leave this vital matter to chance. Economic preparedness is fully as important to the nation as military preparedness.
7.	The chancellor of the exchequer reported to the conference developments during the last year in Europe and in the organization for European economic cooperation, and called attention to the expansion of production and the strengthening of the position of European countries generally.
8.	We also noted that the international monetary fund, in its report to the economic and social council of the United Nations, stated that-
-in order to prevent small depressions from growing into large ones, such supplementary reserves (i.e. international reserves in the international monetary fund) should be supplied early, on liberal terms and in adequate amounts . . . But primary reliance for the avoidance and cure of depressions must be placed upon appropriate measures at the national level, especially in industrial countries.
9.	The sound economic policies pursued by the commonwealth countries, the publicly expressed resolve of the United States government to keep the economy of the United States strong and growing, the expansion of production in Europe, and the substantial increase in monetary reserves outside the dollar area provide, in our judgment, solid grounds for confidence.
Progress in the Short-Term
10.	The conference then discussed current policies, namely:-
(a)	the maintenance of a strong balance of payments position and the strengthening of the central gold and dollar reserves;
(b)	sound internal policies and the need to restrain inflation;
(c)	economic development of resources.
11.	Considerable progress has been made in the application of these policies during the past twelve months, a period when, despite weakness in certain commodity prices, economic conditions have been generally favourable. In the result the over-all deficit in the sterling area balance of payments in 1951-52 was turned into a surplus
in 1952-53, the position of sterling in the world has been strengthened and the central reserves have steadily increased. But we realize that much still remains to be done.
Short-Term Balance of Payments
12.	The policies adopted since the meeting of commonwealth finance ministers in January, 1952, have been at the base of the remarkable change in the balance of payments of the sterling area. In the year ending 30th June, 1953, the sterling area had a surplus of over £400 million in transactions with the outside world, compared with a deficit of nearly £1,000 million in the year ended 30th June, 1952. This marked improvement in the fortunes of the sterling area, to which all members have contributed, brought with it an increase of about £250 million in the central reserves of gold and dollars. These reserves have continued to increase, although rather more slowly, in the second half of 1953, and at the end of the year stood at £900 million. Throughout the period sterling has gained strength.
13.	The conference reviewed the prospects for the coming year. We agreed that the sterling area as a whole would seek to maintain a substantial surplus in its payments with the rest of the world. Earlier the main emphasis was placed on dollar earnings. Although the dollar situation has improved, we should not relax our efforts to achieve a dollar surplus; but it is just as important today that we should earn a substantial surplus in other non-sterling currencies. We recognize that success in these aims will depend in part on the level of world trade, but we emphasize that the primary task of all sterling area countries in the forthcoming year is to increase their earnings by intensive efforts over the whole field of exports.
14.	In this task we must show ingenuity, increased efficiency and competitive strength. We cannot afford to disregard any market, and we must develop our exports wherever we can. While we must continue to expand our traditional major exports, we must also expand our exports of the immense variety of other products which in the aggregate form so large a proportion of the total earnings of the sterling area.
15.	The communique of the commonwealth economic conference in December, 1952, referred to the extensive restrictions which some countries of the sterling commonwealth had needed to impose upon imports from the United Kingdom and other commonwealth sources. There was agreement at that time that these restrictions should be relaxed as the external financial position of these

countries improved. We note with satisfaction the progress in this matter which has since been made by several sterling area countries and the prospects of further progress made possible by continuing improvement in their balances of payments.
Internal Policies
16.	We have reviewed the internal policies of our countries and have observed that considerable improvement has been made during the past year. But more remains to be done and the importance of this part of our task cannot be over-emphasized. On the application of sound economic policies depends the purchasing power of money, the cost of living and the ability to sell exports in increasingly competitive world markets. Shortcomings in the internal policies of any one member affect the external fortunes of the whole sterling area by creating excessive demand for imports, diverting resources from export industries and throwing the balance of payments out of equilibrium. Our governments will continue to follow the policies which have served satisfactorily in the past year. Where necessary they will be adjusted so as to encourage increased production for export and to stimulate savings, upon which the development of the commonwealth substantially depends.
Development
17.	The commonwealth has great resources, natural, human and industrial. The need for their development is urgent, and indeed, vital. The aim of all sterling area commonwealth countries is to concentrate on the development of those resources which, directly or indirectly, contribute on an economic basis towards improving the balance of payments of the sterling area. In some countries of the area, however, development plans have been made to provide for some basic improvement in the standards of living, which is a necessary foundation for further economic development.
18.	The outstanding impression given by the reports made to us by our colleagues is of the immense variety and intensity of the efforts which are being made to turn to productive use the many resources, both large and small, of the commonwealth countries.
19.	It is impossible to describe briefly all these activities. The following are examples. The development of food production has been intensified throughout the commonwealth. This has called for irrigation and other schemes for bringing more land under cultivation, technical improvements, mechanization and training. The production of such commodities as cotton, jute, wool, wood pulp,
Commonwealth Finance Conference timber, tobacco and sisal has been maintained. There has been continued development of the mineral resources of the commonwealth, in particular, uranium, gold, copper, nickel, chrome, asbestos, coal, iron ore and bauxite. The production of some commodities, such as tin and rubber, has been affected by fluctuations in world demand. In a number of countries the search for oil and the development of oil and production of natural gas are in progress. The development of heavy industries continues to have an important place. The expansion of iron and steel production and the production of aluminium are proceeding in a number of countries. A great variety of other industrial development is also taking place. Efforts to improve and extend transport facilities have continued and there has been considerable expenditure on road, railways and harbour works. Substantial programs for increasing electric generating capacity, both thermal and hydroelectric, are in progress. Schemes for improvement of housing, education and health services are under way.
20.	There is much evidence that development has everywhere gone ahead more smoothly and economically as inflation has been checked and excessive competition for resources has been materially lessened. This makes it clear that sound internal policies are just as important to economic growth as they are to a healthy balance of payments.
21.	We have reviewed the factors which affect the scope and pace of development. Supplies of goods for development have much improved. But in most cases finance is still the major factor limiting development. Each of our governments will continue policies designed to secure the highest possible level of internal savings. However most individual countries and the sterling area as a whole still need additional financial resources from outside.
22.	At the commonwealth economic conference of December, 1952, the United Kingdom government undertook to make a special effort to provide additional capital for commonwealth development, in the knowledge that this required an adequate level of internal savings and an adequate surplus in its overseas accounts. In 1953 the United Kingdom government authorized loans and grants totalling £120 million for development in the sterling commonwealth, including the colonial territories for which the United Kingdom has a special responsibility. The loans were made through a number of channels, including the London market, the export credits guarantee department and the colonial development corporation. Grants were

Commonwealth Finance Conference made to the colonial territories from colonial development and welfare funds. The United Kingdom government will continue this policy in 1954, and will make special efforts to develop its own resources. While this involves burdens and risks, the United Kingdom government has consciously undertaken the task in the faith that sound development is the basis of the future prosperity of Britain and the commonwealth, that such development is needed in bad times as in good, and that the provision of finance from the United Kingdom will substantially help its own exports.
23.	Finance from the United Kingdom for commonwealth development flows through many channels. Two new channels were opened up in 1953. The Commonwealth Development Finance Company has started operations, its role being primarily to help the financing of development undertaken by private enterprise. A beginning has also been made in the use of the sterling which the United Kingdom made available for lending through the international bank for reconstruction and development. There are cases however which international bank finance does not fully cover, for example, where development consists of large self-contained projects combined with a mass of small items involving over-all a high proportion of local expenditure. Commonwealth governments may now approach the London market after consultation with the United Kingdom government, not only in relation to particular projects, but also in support of general programs of development, provided the necessary conditions have been fulfilled. In view of the many claims upon this market, including provision for development in the United Kingdom, access has to be limited. The United Kingdom government will therefore wish to be sure, first, that the programs as a whole are in conformity with the general policy of concentrating on the improvement of the sterling area's balance of payments, and secondly, that the country concerned is making an adequate contribution from its own resources. It is also necessary in the general interest for the timing of any such borrowing to be carefully regulated.
24.	We have reaffirmed our determination to press on with development, in conformity with our general policy, to the limit of available resources. In some of our countries private enterprise is making a large contribution to development. Governments will be concerned to promote balanced development, whether public or private, to pursue policies designed to increase the flow of savings, and to encourage private investment from both internal and external sources.

The Collective Approach to Freer Trade and Payments
25.	We reaffirm our support for the proposals, shortly referred to as the collective approach, which emerged from the commonwealth economic conference of December, 1952. These proposals, which are set out in full in paragraphs 17 to 22 of the communique of that conference, are designed in general to bring about the widest possible system of multilateral trade and payments, the reduction and progressive elimination of import restrictions, and the convertibility of sterling and other important currencies. They are based on collective action, by debtor and creditor countries, to bring about a balance in the world economy on the basis of "trade not aid".
26.	The growing confidence in sterling and the increasing strength and flexibility of the economies of the sterling area countries have enabled them to make progress in the move towards expanding trade and freeing currencies. But decisive action must be related to the fulfilment of the conditions indicated in the communique of the commonwealth economic conference. These conditions are:-
(a)	The continuing success of internal policies of sterling commonwealth countries;
(b)	The prospect that trading nations will adopt trade policies which are conducive to the expansion of world trade;
(c)	The availability of adequate financial support, through the international monetary fund or otherwise.
27.	We have noted with great satisfaction the passage in President Eisenhower's recent message to congress in which he referred to the creation of a healthier and freer system of trade and payments in which others could earn their own living and the United States economy could continue to flourish. All commonwealth countries await with interest the detailed recommendations which the President will make to congress after the joint commission on the foreign economic policy of the United States has made its report. While stressing the importance of the policies, external and internal, which our own countries should pursue, we believe that the forthcoming declaration of United States policies will have a profound significance for the free world.
28.	We reaffirm the intention of our governments to work as far as possible through existing international organizations dealing with trade and finance.
29.	The functions which the GATT and the IMF perform will become even more important when moves to freer trade and currencies are concerted; their rules, procedures and organization need close examination and

review in some respects if they are to play a full and effective part. We note the forthcoming review of the GATT and agree that there should be prior consultation among commonwealth countries about this in the light of the circumstances then existing.
30.	The sterling area has a close interest in the European payments union through the membership of the United Kingdom in that union and the use of sterling in it. We will follow with interest the studies now proceeding in the OEEC on convertibility and how a transition can be best effected from the EPU to a wider system of trade and payments.
31.	We conclude by saying something about great, though intangible, matters. We come from the ends of the earth. We represent nations, varying in language, religion, and in tradition, developed or underdeveloped, divided physically by the mountains or by the waste of seas. But we have met not as strangers but as friends. We have not met to discover how we can strengthen each of us himself at the expense of the other, but ourselves as a family of nations. For we have faith in ourselves, and in our future, and in our enduring company,
Commonwealth Finance Conference one with another. Our congress, however, does not end there. We are not a commonwealth of nations, arrayed against the rest of the world. We are for the world. The free world is built upon freedom. Freedom is built upon strength.
32.	The underlying element of thought and feeling at our meeting has been our deep and united faith that the strength of our commonwealth is the strength of freedom; that the freer exchange of currencies and trade can be best assisted by the strength of our own currency and the expansion of our own trade and commerce.
33.	We avow ourselves, and the nations which it is our honour to represent, the friends of peace, the advocates of peaceful trade, the apostles of understanding. We even venture to look forward to the day when the developed wealth of our own nations will serve all others; when trade and prosperity will know no inhuman barriers; when the raising of living standards will be the common endeavour of all; and when the friendly brotherhood which we have experienced in this conference will have become the common lot of mankind.
